speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a brief announcement concerning the financing of Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation. Hon. members will recall that in November, 1955 the former government entered into an agreement with Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited for the construction and rental to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited of the northern Ontario section of an all-Canadian natural gas pipe line.
To launch the project and to enable Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited to enter into contracts to buy and sell gas and to finance construction of its portion of the line, an arrangement between the government of Canada and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited regarding an assured rental of the northern Ontario section on a firm contractual basis was entered into. To determine the rental a firm interest rate was fixed at 3i per cent. Concurrently an agreement was entered into with the province of Ontario whereby the province agreed to lend to the crown corporation which was to be set up to construct the northern Ontario section of the line one-third of the cost or $35 million, whichever might be less.
The interest on the capital investment of the two governments was to be payable at rates related to the respective rates of interest prevailing for outstanding obligations of Ontario and Canada, and was to be agreed upon prior to the commencement of the construction of the northern Ontario section.
Although the lease with Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited was based on a firm interest rate of 3J per cent, no firm arrangements with Ontario were made by the former government regarding the rate of interest on the province's share of the advances, and in the absence of any agreement on the interest rate no advances have been made by the province of Ontario. Consequently the crown corporation has been financed entirely by advances by Canada. To the 31st January, 66968-9-40
1959 we have advanced a total of $112,750,000 to Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation.
In the course of recent discussions concerning the rate of interest which was to be paid on any advances that might be made by the province of Ontario, Premier Frost has taken the position that Ontario should not be called upon to make any advances to the crown corporation at anything less than the going rate of interest; that is to say, the rate of interest which the province of Ontario itself must pay on moneys it borrows, and that rate is somewhat higher than the rates prevailing at the time the original agreement was made and construction commenced, and certainly higher than the 3| per cent rate.
We have searched the records carefully and can find no place where in any discussion or any exchange of correspondence which occurred between the government of Canada and the government of the province of Ontario there was any stipulation on the part of the former federal government as to the rate of interest at which the loan was to be made by the province of Ontario; and having nothing in that respect to rely upon the government has concluded that as the main pipe line of the northern Ontario section has been substantially completed on the basis of federal funds-although there will be some additional capital outlay for compressor stations-and as gas is now flowing through the lines, there is no point now in asking the province to advance any share of the moneys as originally agreed.
The fact is that if the province of Ontario were to advance moneys to this crown corporation at the rate of interest which it must pay on its public borrowings it would simply mean a deficit on the part of this crown corporation which the federal treasury would have to make good. Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, the government has decided that under the circumstances it has no alternative but to provide all the funds required to complete the construction of the northern Ontario section of the pipe line.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON TALKS HELD IN WASHINGTON ON JANUARY 29

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: STATEMENT ON TALKS HELD IN WASHINGTON ON JANUARY 29
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to give the house a brief report on the talks held in Washington
618	HOUSE OF
Statement on Canadian Radio Patents Ltd. on Thursday, January 29, between myself and Hon. William P. Rogers, Attorney General of the United States, concerning the extraterritorial effects of actions launched in United States courts under United States antitrust laws.
I was accompanied by Mr. T. D. MacDonald, director of investigation and research of our Department of Justice and by officials of the Canadian embassy in Washington. On the United States side, in addition to Mr. Rogers, the talks were attended by senior officials of his department and by an official of the United States state department. For the background of the discussion I should refer hon. members to my statement on January 19, 1959, reported on page 25 of Hansard. The talks were held in accordance with the arrangements outlined there.
In the course of those talks I outlined our concern about the effects in Canada of antitrust actions commenced by the United States government in United States courts. While our concern in this matter is of general application, it was illustrated and discussed particularly in the light of the current antitrust suit commenced on November 24, 1958, in which three companies in the United States are named as defendants and a number of companies incorporated in Canada are named as co-conspirators.
This suit arises out of the alleged activities of all of these companies in connection with a Canadian organization known as Canadian Radio Patents Limited. This is a company which was formed in 1926, to which the leading companies in Canada have assigned their patent rights. This company has in general licensed those patents only to firms intending to manufacture in Canada, and it is a significant fact that this organization has never since its inception been charged with any offence against any Canadian law. It is also significant that we have in Canada today a healthy and expanding radio and television appliance manufacturing industry, and that only a very small proportion of Canadian domestic requirements in this field is imported from the United States.
In the course of our discussions I made it clear that I was not commenting on the merits of the antitrust case in the United States in so far as it sought only to bring United States law to bear upon United States companies in respect of their conduct in the United States. I also made it clear that I was not discussing the merits of Canadian Radio Patents Limited as such.
I emphasized that what we are concerned about is the possible effect of the decree asked for in the United States in so far as it may require directors of Canadian companies to take certain actions with respect


to the operations of those companies in Canada, which actions would not be dictated by the requirements of Canadian law, or be in accord with Canadian business or commercial policy, but would be dictated by requirements of United States law and be in accord with United States policy.
I made clear that in our view such a result could only be regarded as an infringement of Canadian sovereignty. I suggested that if the United States government has any feeling that actions in Canada in this or in any other field are counter to United States interests or involve any infringement of arrangements with respect to commerce between our two countries, the proper course for them is not to seek to alter the situation in Canada by means of unilateral action in United States courts, but rather to raise the problem with the Canadian government and express their views through the usual channels.
I further stated that it is our view that in matters of this sort the ultimate decision as to what is done in Canada must be the responsibility of the Canadian government, and that we felt that the answer to the problem lies in the exercise of restraint by the United States government in seeking from their courts or applying measures that interfere directly, substantially and deliberately with matters that are essentially matters of Canadian commerce within Canada.
In particular, I emphasized our view that to follow any other course could only be based on the unacceptable proposition that foreign subsidiaries of United States parent companies are merely projections of United States trade and commerce and subject to United States policy in priority to the laws and commercial interests of the countries in which such subsidiaries are incorporated and carry on business.
The United States Attorney General assured me that the action taken by the United States government in this or any other antitrust suit is not taken by them with any intent of infringing the sovereignty of Canada but is taken only in discharge of the responsibility resting on their government to enforce the United States antitrust laws in their own country. He expressed the view that no threat to Canadian sovereignty is involved and also his concern that the contrary view should have been taken. He emphasized that the United States government did not take the position that United States laws should supersede the laws of any other country, but acted only in accordance with what it regarded as its obligation to ensure that all persons in any way subject to the

United States laws, including American antitrust laws, lived and acted in accordance therewith.
As a result of these talks it was readily agreed that in any similar situation in the future, discussions will be held between the two governments at the appropriate stage when it becomes apparent that interests in one of our countries are likely to be affected by the enforcement of the antitrust laws of the other. Such discussions would be designed to explore ways and means of avoiding the sort of situation which would give rise to objections or misunderstandings in the other country. It was, however, made clear that each government would have to reserve its ultimate responsibility to decide for itself what action it should take, and that such consultations should not be regarded in any way as necessarily implying approval of the action ultimately taken.
I believe that the arrival at an understanding on prior consultation is a real accomplishment. At the same time I do not wish to over remphasize the extent or effect of this understanding regarding consultation. It should be realized that there was revealed in the course of these discussions, a wide divergence between our two views as to what amounts to an infringement of sovereignty and as to the restraint which one country should exercise in seeking decrees from its own courts when those decrees may have effects within another country. Until there is a satisfactory reconciliation of views on these points there can be no guarantee that causes for complaint will not arise again.
While I believe that I should in fairness place these facts squarely before the house, nevertheless I repeat that in my view the talks may prove an important and useful first step toward an improvement in the situation, by enabling each side to understand what is the other's point of view, and by opening the door to further consultation which may in turn lay the ground for progress in the reconciliation of those views.

speechtext:
As we of
the C.C.F. have said on other occasions, Mr. Speaker, we feel it is most regrettable that companies in Canada which are subsidiaries of United States companies would appear to be required to follow laws laid down in the United States, contrary to the policy of the Canadian government and contrary to Canadian law. Without talking at this moment about the principles involved, I can say most emphatically that we agree with the principle that companies in Canada should follow Canadian law only and should not be required in any way, shape or form, to follow laws laid down in foreign countries.
We think it is time the Canadian government not only talked in this manner to the United States, but considered introducing in our parliament a law which would make it crystal clear that companies operating in Canada must obey Canadian laws and must operate in our commercial interests. In addition, it should be made clear that in any instance in which there appears to be a conflict between the commercial interest of this nation and the law of some other country, our law and our commercial interest only should apply.
Perhaps this is a difficult subject upon which to make this kind of statement, because there is evidence that we have in Canada a trust so far as the Canadian radio patents pool is concerned. I want to point out immediately that the Ilsley royal commission is inquiring into this subject and will be making a report to parliament. It may be that Canada should take its own action so far as the monopoly in this field is concerned, but that in no way detracts from the statement I have made that in principle Canadian law and Canadian interest only should govern the actions of Canadian companies.
I want to repeat to the minister a request we made in this house in another form and on another occasion. I do this not in any

We do feel that the minister is thoroughly justified in laying down the principle he has laid down at this time. We hope, we trust and we expect that the method of handling these disputes in the future will be more satisfactory to Canada than the result of similar assurances given in this house last year.

Mr. Chairman, under the heading of this vote I should like to bring to the attention of the committee the seriousness of the current rabies epidemic in southern-central Ontario. I would ask the minister to bear in mind the seriousness of the losses suffered by farmers in that part of this province. The majority of the farmers there are engaged in dairy farming and in the raising of beef cattle for marketing, and it is here

that the disease has been most rampant. Certain measures have been taken by the department to curb the spread of this disease through the biting of untamed and domestic animals, and various steps have been taken by the local authorities as well to prevent the spread of the disease. In consideration of the losses being sustained, however, I feel that some other measure of assistance should be considered.
There were 2,218 cases of rabies reported in Canada in 1958. Of this number 896 were reported in Ontario and were diagnosed through the federal laboratory. In addition there were a further 169 cases in Ontario that were clinically diagnosed by government veterinarians in various areas.
In my own riding of Grey-Bruce 178 cattle were lost to December 31, not to mention the considerable number of other animals including sheep, horses and others, with an additional 50 clinical cases diagnosed. This represents a considerable loss to the farmers in that area, and I know that other hon. gentlemen report a similar experience in their ridings.
I am aware of the statements that have been issued by the department, and I am familiar with the attitude of the department in this respect. The department realizes that the disease is not spread by the livestock themselves but is spread mainly by foxes and other such animals, and there is no discretionary authority for the minister to compensate for these losses.
In view of the seriousness of the epidemic I would ask the minister and his department to give consideration to paying compensation in those cases. My suggestion and the considered suggestion of farm organizations and farmers themselves in representations that have been made to me is that a flat sum outside of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act be considered as compensation for those farmers, and that it be provided through some enabling legislation under which the federal government would pay one-third, the provincial government one-third and the county level of government one-third. I would ask for the sincere consideration of the minister and his department in this particular case.

Mr. Chairman, in regard to the question just asked as to an indication of what this particular amount of $400,000 is for, during the present fiscal year we have greatly stepped up the tuberculosis and especially the brucellosis eradication programs. This became particularly necessary because of a change in the United States health of animals regulations which was put into effect in November, and which made more stringent the regulations as far as the United States was concerned concerning those two diseases as applying to cattle which were imported into the United Sates. Therefore in order to protect our position and leave us in a position to export cattle from here to the United States we had to improve or increase our brucellosis and tuberculosis testing programs. That is one of the reasons why this extra $400,000 is required this year. We started last summer with a very greatly expedited program of brucellosis testing particularly.
The other reason that more money is required is that hon. members will recall that at the last session of parliament we increased the rate of compensation for cattle slaughtered under those two programs from $40 to $70 for grade animals and from $100 to $140 for pure bred animals. Those two things combined have caused the need for this $400,000 more than was provided in the main estimates.
In regard to the matter of rabies, which was brought up, the proposition the hon. member for Grey-Bruce has put forward that the municipal authorities, the provincial authorities and the federal government should compensate the owners of animals which have died as a result of rabies seems reasonable. It is one which, if the municipalities and the provinces wish to put it up, I will be prepared to look at very seriously. Up to date I have had no representations along that line from either municipal or provincial authorities.
However, as the hon. member indicated, under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act there just is no provision for payment of compensation for animals which die from rabies or from any other such diseases. The whole purpose of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act is to eradicate or control contagious diseases which are passed from cattle and other animals, from one to the other. Rabies do not fall in that class. This disease is spread chiefly by foxes, part of the wild life of the country. The chief danger from rabies and the chief means of control which we have
Supply-Agriculture
exercised is to prevent rabies from becoming common in the dog population. If a considerable number of dogs contracted rabies, then we would have a very rapid spread of the disease by dogs biting one another and biting human beings.
We have not had one single case of transmission of rabies from dog to dog. That has been prevented by control measures exercised by the municipalities, and by the inoculation or vaccination clinics which we have carried on in every county in Ontario in which rabies have become a threat. We are continuing to carry on those clinics. We think the disease is dying down, and we hope it will die down very rapidly during the coming few months.
As far as the general subject of compensation is concerned, on which I may say I have received a large number of letters, I regret to say there is no power under the act as it stands to pay compensation for animals which die from rabies.

This is just not the case. The total number of cattle in Canada that died in that period was 720. While it is a considerable number and is very regrettable, the situation is not nearly as serious as many people believe.

I should like to congratulate the minister on putting this item of $400,000 in these estimates, but it is just a drop of water in the bucket compared with the expense the government is going to have to face this year. I would be pleased if the minister would secure more veterinarians in order to deal with brucellosis. In my riding of Russell the department does not have nearly enough doctors. Please use this money to get more doctors. We need this protection in order to be able to sell our cattle to the United States. If we do not have the United States market the farmers will suffer greatly, because only when they can ship their cattle to the United States can they manage to make a living.
I am not in favour of the motion of one hon. member that the municipality should pay one-third of the cost of the animal dying from rabies. Let us pass a law; we are here for that purpose. Let us pass a law that the government should pay so much for these cattle. Never mind about cats and dogs; take care of the cattle. I congratulate the minister on raising the payments from $40 to $70 and $100 to $140 for cattle destroyed under the tuberculosis and brucellosis programs. He should have raised the amounts more, because when the farmer is forced to sell his cattle he has to do so in order that the meat and milk the people in the cities consume will be free from tuberculosis. The farmer is forced to sell his cattle when they

are condemned by the doctor. He is given practically nothing for his cattle. Any cow is worth $200. He is paid $70, and he sells the carcass for $50. Therefore he has lost $80 for the benefit of the Canadian people.
I think the payment for a milk cow should be $100 instead of $70; otherwise the farmer will take a big loss. He will not be able to ship to the United States if the department does not get as many veterinarians as possible and do the job right now. If the minister will do this it will be a very good thing not only for the farmers of my riding but for the farmers of all Canada who want to ship their cattle to the United States in order to get a good price.

I think I should point out that the hon. member for Russell is under a misapprehension if he thinks that all a man gets for a cow that has to be slaughtered is $70. In addition he gets the value of the carcass, and in most cases the value of the carcass is not much less than if the animal had not had brucellosis or had just been slaughtered in the ordinary way. The result is that in many cases the farmer gets more for the animal than if he had sold it commercially. The hon. member has said that the payment should be much higher. He has said that the animal is worth $200 and therefore the farmer should get $200, but in effect this would mean that he would be paid twice for the animal. I think the present level of payment is very generous indeed.
I know what I am talking about and what the farmers in my riding have received. They have had to sell cattle for $30, $40 or $50, and I say they should be paid at least $100.
Mr. Chairman, the minister indicated the number of cattle and other animals that died last year, and I should like him to give us the figures for the two previous years.

I have not the figures here for those years, but the numbers were considerably less. As a matter of fact, the year before last losses of cattle and so on were chiefly in the province of Quebec and to some extent in northern Ontario, and for two or three years before that the losses were almost entirely in western Canada.

I think I am correct in saying that the number of cattle that died throughout Canada in the previous year was 101. Last year there were over 700. That would indicate that there was a lot more rabies in the country this year than last year, and I think special consideration should be given to the situation. In my own riding 126 cattle have died in the last year, and 78 humans have
Supply-Agriculture
been treated for rabies. I have one farmer who lost 9 cattle, and several who have lost 3. The minister may not think it is important to these farmers, but I certainly feel it is. It is quite a blow to the farmer who lost 9 cattle. It is something over which he has no control.
I notice that the province of Ontario has agreed to start a vaccination program for animals at present in barns so that when they go out they will be immune to attacks of wild animals, but that does not help the farmers who are having trouble right now. As a matter of fact, some cattle put in barns last October are dying of rabies in the barn.
In my opinion special consideration should be given to the situation. If compensation were paid the farmers would be more careful. The fact that there is a 60-day quarantine period makes the farmer feel that he cannot sell anything off his farm. He feels that he is going to have trouble selling; therefore when he sees an animal that he thinks might have rabies he sells it. Who is to say that the meat from the animal is not consumed by humans, or that the animal does not reach the stockyards where some of the handlers may get the disease?
I think the act could be changed in some way to make it possible to pay compensation. After all, a farmer whose sheep have been worried by dogs is paid for the sheep that die. That is not his responsibility, and here is a situation with regard to cattle that is no responsibility of the farmer. It does not arise through neglect on his part. Therefore I think the government should give special consideration to the situation and see if compensation cannot be arranged.

I can only repeat that the purpose of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act is to prevent the spread of disease, and to pay compensation for cattle affected with rabies would not fall in that category. I have every sympathy with people who have lost cattle or other animals as the result of rabies. It is a very severe blow. As the hon. member has just stated, every year throughout Canada there are thousands of cattle which die, and there is no more reason to pay compensation for an animal that dies from rabies than for an animal that dies from any other cause. Unless we want to adopt a different policy so far as the health of animals is concerned and pay compensation for every animal that dies, no matter what the cause may be, I do not see any good reason for completely changing the basis of the act in order to start paying compensation for rabies.
I feel that the proposition put forward by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce might be a reasonable way to handle this rabies problem.

If some proposition along that line were put forward to the Department of Agriculture, as I said before, we will certainly be glad to consider it seriously. As I say, the basis for the payment of compensation under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act is so that people will be encouraged to come forward if they have a sick animal, it may be foot-and-mouth disease or some other contagious disease. We pay them if that animal is slaughtered, and in this way we prevent a spread of contagious diseases and people are encouraged to assist in wiping out these diseases. That is the whole basis of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, and I do not think it would be reasonable to start paying compensation for any animal that dies from any cause.

I should like to express my agreement with the hon. member for Welling-ton-Huron as well as the hon. member for Grey-Bruce. There is a great deal of concern amongst the agricultural people of Ontario over the fact that they are not being compensated properly for animals they lose.
I should like to refer to one disease, brucellosis. As the minister explained a moment ago, if compensation were paid for beef cattle it is quite true that the meat

would be worth nearly as much after the compensation was paid as it was before. However, brucellosis is not a disease that affects beef cattle to the same extent that it affects dairy cattle. In so far as dairy cattle are concerned, at the last Holstein sale in Ontario the average price for a cow was $375. A dairy cow selling for meat will bring less than $200. I feel, therefore, the farmer is not getting what he considers to be fair compensation for his animals.
In the matter of rabies, I think the federal government has some responsibility. While it is true that one cow does not pass on this disease to another, the disease is continually being spread. It may be necessary for the government to implement a program of eradication of rabies in the province. I feel that the provincial government of Ontario should be congratulated on the vaccine they are making available for the control of the disease. A great deal more effort must be put into it to see that the wild life of the country do not carry this disease, because it seems odd that it spreads into Quebec one year, the next year into Ontario and another year it is in the west. I think there is some justification for the farmer saying that it is not his responsibility because his cow dies from this disease. It is a contagious disease and the cow did not develop it; she caught it from some other source.
The minister also pointed out how many cattle died. I think it is not fair to use the figures he used. I am quite sure he will agree with me that if you had seven or eight cows die, you would only send in one head. If the veterinary treated some across the way he would say, "I just treated the neighbour's cattle, and we sent in one head and this cow died of rabies. Therefore your seven or eight cows that are dying also probably have the disease".
I think this disease has much more importance than we sometimes attach to it. I am sure that more money can be spent on this matter in order to see whether an eradication program can be implemented in order to rid Canada of this terrible problem of rabies. On the other hand I should like to say this in connection with the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. While the farmer is appreciative of any increase that has been made-and we are appreciative of the one that was made last year-there still has not been taken into consideration, particularly in the case of brucellosis, the matter of pure bred cattle and extremely expensive dairy cattle. The amount that is allowed will in no way replace the animal that has to be destroyed.

Along with the hon. member for Grey-Bruce and also the hon. member for
Supp ly-Agriculture
Wellington-Huron, being up in a district that has been in about the centre of the rabies outbreak for the last eight months, I should like to make a few remarks. This problem is extremely serious in our district. I have had several resolutions from people there asking for compensation. Why not?

They made certain allegations in connection with it, and those allegations were not sustained at all when the matter was investigated by the agriculture committee.

Supply-Agriculture
It was with regard to the comparatively low compensation for pure-bred cattle, as compared to the sheep involved, and that is a vastly different thing.

As to the hon. member for Timiskaming, he said we should do something about wild life through which rabies spread. I should like to point out to him that the dominion government has no control over wild life except in the Northwest Territories, and has no responsibility for and no power to do anything in connection with wild life except in those areas. The wild life is one of the natural resources which are under the control of the provinces.
At one time we had in mind putting on a poisoning campaign or making a contribution to a poisoning campaign in connection with foxes; but the Ontario wild life authorities, taking into consideration the number of dogs that would probably have been poisoned, the danger to children and to other wild life of all kinds, felt that it was too dangerous a way to try to cope with the matter, and I think probably they were right. In any event the eradication of foxes, which are the chief means by which rabies is spread, is in the hands of the provinces and not in the hands of the dominion.

He said that brucellosis is not of particular concern to beef producers but that it is chiefly of concern to dairy producers. That statement of course is completely incorrect. Most of our exports of cattle to the United States, as a matter of fact, are beef cattle; and it is particularly in order to protect our exports of beef cattle to the United States that we have been obliged to step up, as we have, our brucellosis eradication campaign.

I do not want to hold up the committee, Mr. Chairman, but I want to make a few comments on this matter. First of all I should like to express agreement with the hon. member for Grey-Bruce that perhaps we could have a program of co-operation with the various provinces right across the country. As the hon. member has said, this act will not cover the rabies losses, and quite rightly so. This is an act to prevent the spread of disease. One of the hon. members in the opposition made some remark about foot-and-mouth disease. Just in order to give an idea of the importance of Canada's health of animals division in the government, may I say that the loss to Canadian cattlemen through foot-and-mouth disease in Canada was something in 
the nature of $600 million. Fortunately this government has taken the lead in a campaign to wipe out brucellosis, which could mean as much in savings to the cattlemen in Canada as was lost through the foot-and-mouth disease a number of years ago.

I have only one suggestion that I should like to put forward. The fact is that we in Canada require more men who are trained in veterinary medicine. I would suggest that if at all possible the federal government give some consideration to a grant to a veterinary college in western Canada.

Is it because there were greater quantities of feed grain moved requiring assistance of this kind? What part of this amount, if any, has to do with increases in freight rates?

There are two reasons for this increase. The first is that the volume of feed grain which was moved last year was considerably in excess of the quantities moved in the preceding two or three years. As a result, about $1,500,000 extra-I think it is somewhere in that neighbourhood-is required because of the increased volume of grain being shipped from western Canada to the east and to British Columbia under the freight rate assistance policy. I have the figures here. To the end of December, this year's volume was 2,029,000 tons compared with 1,815,000 tons in the previous year.
The second reason is to compensate for the increase in freight rates. When the 17 per cent increase in freight rates went into effect, had no action been taken it would have thrown out of balance the payment of assistance on feed grains. The payments were made on quite a complicated basis and I do not think we should take the time to go into it here, but the final result was

Supp ly-A griculture
that a 100 pound bag of feed in British Columbia, in Ontario and in the maritime provinces was sold at approximately the same price. There might have been a difference of five or ten cents between one town and another, but the price of a 100 pound bag of feed was approximately the same everywhere.
When the increase in freight rates came into effect we made adjustments under which about half the increase was absorbed by the taxpayer, and it was absorbed in such a way as to keep the cost of 100 pounds of feed at relatively the same price in the three areas to which this feed grain is shipped.

I should like to make a few general remarks on this item and on the way in which the feed grain subsidy has been applied over the years. They will be quite brief. There have been sometimes arguments in this house about which area of Canada the freight subsidy helps most. I would imagine that if the economists went into this very carefully they would say that the greatest benefit went to the feeders in the remote parts of Canada. But without endeavouring to assess the proportionate benefits that accrue as between the feeders and the producers I wish to state that this is' one action taken by the government that has definitely been of benefit to the producers of feed grains and the livestock producers of this country. We are pleased to support this item as we have over the years supported items of freight assistance.
I must point out, however, that this particular policy is becoming a casualty of inflation. I say this for the following reason. I believe this was first implemented in 1941 and during the period from 1941 to 1948 the federal government generally paid the total cost of moving feed grains from Fort William to the basing points. The subsidy in those years was $6, the basic rate to the Montreal zone.
From what year?
From 1941 to 1948, if the information I have is correct and I believe it is.
It was established in 1941?

Yes. The subsidy paid the
entire cost of moving freight under this formula which was arrived at by averaging the lake and rail rates with the all-rail rate so the flat average in general was adequate to meet the cost of moving feed grains.
In 1948 there was an increase in freight rates. With each subsequent increase in
[Mr. Harkness.l
freight rates since that time the effect of the freight rate subsidy has gradually become less. Again my figures may be in error but I have been careful in my computation and I believe they are correct. My figures indicate that since 1948-since the time of the first increase in freight rates-there have been increases in freight rates on feed grains totalling 184 per cent. That is the measure of inflation as it has affected freight rates in reference to feed grains. Prior to 1948, as I have said, the subsidy was $6. This was reduced to $4.50 at a later date.
I thought that after 1953 the average was around $8?

There are two types of subsidy. One is the subsidy from Fort William to the main basing point. The other is the subsidy from that area to some other area and the arbitraries which are the subsidies from the basing area to the final destination have been fully paid. I am now talking about the main basic rate from Fort William to Montreal.
In March, 1957 under the Liberal administration the reduced rate of $4.50 in the form of a subsidy payment was increased by 50 cents to $5 a hundredweight. Since that time the $5 payment has remained the same until this recent increase of $1 on this base formula because of a 10 cent per hundredweight increase in freight rates-$2 a ton- and the government by this vote is absorbing half of that cost. At the present time the current base rate from Fort William to the Montreal zone is 71 cents a hundredweight or $14.20 a ton. The subsidy that is paid is $6 and so the subsidy which once covered the total cost on this basis now covers just 42 per cent of the cost even though the $1 increase in the freight subsidy now being paid brings the subsidy to $6 which is the same as the payment from 1941 to 1948.
The item we are asked to pass today is one which I am sure will commend itself to all hon. members of the committee. We are pleased to support this item. No matter what argument may be advanced as to what group or area may derive the greatest benefit from it I believe it is a good policy and one that helps maintain the price of feed grains to producers in western Canada. At the same time, as the minister has pointed out, this serves to keep the final or retail price to feeders in the maritimes, Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia at the same level. However, because the entire problem of inflation has not been dealt with effectively the subsidy now amounts to only 42 per cent of the total cost involved despite the fact that the subsidy now is as high as it was during and after the war. This is working a hardship on the feed producers and grain producers of

western Canada because what was in earlier days the payment of the cost of transportation over this bridge has now been reduced to just 42 per cent of the cost.
I am glad that the minister has agreed to take up a part of the 17 per cent increase in freight rates and I express the hope that in keeping with the general announcement in the speech from the throne as to action that will be taken to reduce the effect of increased freight rates across this country the situation I have outlined will be kept in line.

Mr. Chairman, this is a very complicated matter and I do not think we should attempt at the moment to go into it in detail. However, I should not like to leave the impression that may be created by one statement made by the hon. member for Assiniboia. I believe if he examines the question in more detail he will change his opinion. The hon. gentleman has said that the subsidy being paid represents only 42 per cent of the total cost and his figures may be accurate. However, in actual fact most of the feed grain goes to the province of Ontario and the western part of Quebec and most of it is carried by water. The subsidy of $5 a ton covers the entire cost of the freight from Fort William to quite a number of ports around the lakes. I mention that simply to correct the impression conveyed by the hon. gentleman's remark that the subsidy was now paying only 42 per cent of the amount of the freight that it was paying approximately ten years ago. The biggest bulk of the freight goes by water transport and the subsidy fully pays the cost.
I thank the minister for the contribution he has made.
That is mighty white of you.

I do not know what the joke is about, Mr. Chairman. I do not know how it helps the people in the maritime provinces to have the assurance of the minister that the subsidy covers the cost of transportation of feed grain to parts of Ontario. I do not know how it becomes a joke that the people in British Columbia do not have the advantage of water transportation. I am not endeavouring to become involved in an argument with the minister and I accept the statement he has made.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

Mr. Chairman, if some of the minister's energetic supporters would get up and say something that the Hansard reporter could take down it might be more effective.
Supp ly-A griculture
As I said, I agree with the minister's statement. As far as the main basing point of Montreal is concerned, I believe the statistics are accurate and I accept the minister's statement.

Mr. Chairman, the minister said the beneficiaries of the legislation introduced in 1941 are largely Ontario and Quebec. Is that a correct statement? Taking into consideration the population on a proportionate basis I should think the minister's statement would have to be modified. Surely this benefits the maritime provinces considerably.
There is no question about that at all. It also benefits the province of British Columbia.
Under another measure?
Under the same measure exactly.
I thought it was another.

No. The point I was making was that the bulk of those subsidies is paid on account of grain which is fed in Ontario and Quebec, because it is in Ontario and Quebec that we find the bulk of livestock. Naturally you would expect that. I was also pointing out that as far as Ontario and Quebec are concerned, most of the grain is moved down by water and therefore the subsidy covers the great proportion of the total cost; in some cases it covers all of the cost. This is one of the things that made it difficult to make any adjustments in regard to this after the increase in freight rates, and still keep the cost of a hundred pound bag of feed relatively the same throughout the different areas. Also, in connection with what the hon. member for Assiniboia said, that the help amounted to only 42 per cent, this is not correct because in Ontario-
On the basic rate, I said; the arbitraries are paid entirely.

In the province of New Brunswick, for example, the freight from the lakehead is $22.40, and the assistance which is provided under this act is $15.70, so that the percentage which is paid by the taxpayer really under this act is 70 per cent rather than 42 per cent.

Nobody is quarrelling with that; nobody is saying anything but that. The minister did not give the best example that he might have. I understand the best example is Sydney, Nova Scotia-

No, Newfoundland is the best example.
Well,-
More assistance is paid on grain going to Newfoundland than to anyplace else.

The minister had better inform somebody in his department that Newfoundland is in confederation. I got my information from the same source as he did. My information is that the total cost to Sydney, Nova Scotia, is $24.40, and the subsidy amounts to $17.07. But initially it is made up of the base rate to Montreal, plus, as I said to the member for Essex East, the arbitraries, that is the amount from the base point to the actual point of destination which is fully paid.

Item agreed to.
698. To provide for payments to western grain producers of $1.00 per acre up to a maximum of 200 acres per farm in accordance with regulations of the governor in council-further amount required, $1,300,000.

Mr. Chairman, hon. members are not used to my speaking at any length on an agricultural item. I do so, of course, at this time with some humility and trepidation but with no apology. It is known that my constituency, in so far as members of the Liberal party are concerned, is the one nearest to the grain-growing people of the western provinces.
And you are in Ontario.

I am, of course, prairie-born and prairie-raised and the constituents of Kenora-Rainy River have a great dependence upon the prosperity of western agriculture because I think there are more railway divisional points in my riding than perhaps in the riding of any member in the House of Commons. A large and successful movement of grain through our constituency is of the utmost importance to us.
This is an item that is strictly of benefit to the people of western Canada. I have another reason to be interested in a matter of this kind involving a contribution based on national necessity to a national industry of importance because, as hon. members well know, in the constituency of Kenora-Rainy River we have a substantial production of gold. For a long time, on this basis, where there is an exceptional national industry in temporary need of help we have had a formula for assistance to gold mines and I can assure the house that it has been extremely successful. In so far as our mines are concerned, when the policy was in-


troduced their production was just about one-third of what it is at the present time. In addition to that, I think every mine in the Red Lake district was at one time in receipt of the emergency gold mining assistance which was provided some years ago. I am very happy to say that now, after the passage of time only one, the smallest producer of gold in Kenora-Rainy River, is today requiring any assistance.
On a point of order, this is an item covering the payment of $1 an acre up to a maximum of $200 to western grain producers. The hon. member is speaking entirely on gold subsidies.
I have completed the reference by an analogy.
I can understand that he would be speaking on gold subsidies but I do not think he should do it on this particular item.

I was simply establishing the analogy of the payments to a national industry for the purpose of assisting it through a period of national emergency. I am through with that reference and I want to hasten to say that we are concerned with this particular item because the question of Canadian agriculture, and western agriculture in particular, was very much before us in the recent election campaigns. The Prime Minister very properly, as a longtime member of the house, made it quite clear that he had no lack of understanding of western grain requirements and problems and he painted a very glowing picture of the kind of measures that would be expected from an administration that he would head. We all admit that the Prime Minister is a great artist in colours and he can accompany that painting with proper thespian touches. They were very convincing indeed, if the vote in western Canada is to be remembered, as most of us remember it. But, if rising costs are the yardstick of inflation, I think it certainly can be said that the farmers are one group who have carried on a very obstinate and a very difficult fight against inflation.
I think the people of western Canada- and I visited there rather extensively in the recess between the sessions-are wondering just how long we have to wait for the long range program which has been talked about in so far as improving the condition of western grain producers is concerned. If we heard anything as an indication of the likely policy of the new government with respect to agriculture and western grain producers, we always heard the ringing phrase from the Prime Minister that an administration under him would provide to

iarmers a fair share of the national income. These are the words he repeated so often.
It has been drawn to my attention that the assistance under this particular provision, temporary though it was announced it would be, probably amounts to one-sixth of one per cent of the national income. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, there was every reason for the agricultural community to leap to the conclusion that a Conservative administration would divert a great deal more of the national wealth to their purposes than seems to be provided under this particular measure. Quite irrespective of any legal niceties such as we heard in the debate last session when this item was under consideration on August 30 and on September 6, and irrespective of any legal niceties we may get from the Prime Minister or from the Minister of Agriculture in defining deficiency payments, parity and the like now, there is no doubt in my mind- and I think most members from western Canada will agree-that most of the voters in western Canada certainly had in their minds glowing deficiency payments and parity about which they heard so much from the Prime Minister, not only during his entire career in parliament but in particular during the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958.

Mr. Chairman, once more on a point of order, none of this has anything to do with this $1 an acre acreage payment. I would ask the hon. member to stay within the rules of the house and stay with this topic which we are discussing rather than going into gold mining assistance and general statements.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I have been listening very carefully to the hon. member and I should like to refer him to May, 16th edition, page 738. Under the heading "On Supplementary and Excess Grants" there is the following:
Debate on supplementary and excess grants is restricted to the particulars contained in the estimates on which those grants are sought, and to the application of the items which compose those grants; and the debate cannot touch the policy or the expenditure sanctioned, on other heads, by the estimate on which the original grant was obtained, except so far as such policy or expenditure is brought before the committee by the items contained in the supplementary or excess estimates.
I am sure that the hon. member realizes what that means.

I have every desire to keep within the rules and am familiar with that rule. I suggest that the chair will find that I am adhering to that rule. You will recall that this was a completely new policy even if it was announced that it was to be short lived. You will also remember that the debate with respect to it took place on
Supply-Agriculture
the last day of the last session. You will recall that there was considerable discussion about such matters as its equation with parity, deficiency payments and matters of that kind that are still under very active discussion by the people of western Canada. My point is that we have constantly had difficulties relating the policy of this new administration represented by this $1 per acre grant to parity based on a fair price-cost relationship. My suggestion is that this proposal and extension of it by this additional vote is not arriving at that avowed purpose.
As we have just come back from a recess I am sure that the committee would want to discuss the reaction encountered by members visiting in western Canada since this policy was debated on the last day of the last session. It was announced, I believe on August 30. In my experience I have found, as so often happens in the case of something that is admittedly a stopgap and a rather desperate expedient by way of delay before a final policy is decided upon, it receives probably less appreciation and less thanks than criticism. That has certainly been my experience in western Canada with regard to the comments that have been made to me about this legislation. The best that has been said about it is that it is merely a sign of recognition that some help is needed. That is the best I have heard about it. When the Canadian Federation of Agriculture made its submission to the federal-provincial agricultural conference last November it had this to say:
There is general recognition of the importance of wheat in the national economy. While special payments are being made to grain producers by the government of Canada these payments do not bear any relationship to a long range price support policy for wheat.
I imagine that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture would probably admit that is so. But the question is how soon are we likely to have unfolded, so far as monetary compensation is concerned, the proposals of the government with respect to its long range policy? When the Prime Minister was referring to the long range policy on August 30 last he gave an indication that it involved several categories. The speech from the throne simply refers to the possibility this session of having a new measure with respect to crop insurance and it refers also to some reorganization of credit facilities for agriculture. But there is nothing there to indicate that we are likely to get a measure on a long term basis in substitution for this admittedly temporary measure.

I am sure that the hon. and experienced member for Kenora-Rainy River will once more understand what that means.

I go on with a point which apparently met with your approval. I refer to some of the comments that have been made with respect to the value of this particular type of legislation which we are asked to increase and continue. The Saskatchewan wheat pool made this comment, as found in the Regina Leader-Post of September 3, 1958:
It charged Prime Minister Diefenbaker with failing to realize the seriousness of the situation by implementing a relief measure for one year only when he has admitted in the past that only a long range program can succeed.
I think that most members from western Canada would admit that one of the most important things for western agriculture and the products grown there in abundance which depend on markets beyond our shores is an active and buoyant trade policy. I also think that many people in western Canada, as a result of certain actions taken by the government last session, are very apprehensive about the result of trade policies such as expressed in the increase in the tariff on wool and the difficulties and complaints we are having from the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend may not intend it but in effect what he is doing is simply defying the ruling of the chair. It was bad enough to go into a discussion of gold subsidies on this item but now the hon. member is even farther afield, this after having his attention drawn to the rule several times by you, Mr. Chairman. This is neither a continuation of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne nor is it consideration by the committee of the administration item of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. What is before the committee at this moment is item 698 which relates purely and simply to an additional sum of $1,300,000 required to carry out a program approved by parliament last September, and surely this does not warrant any hon. member going outside a discussion of the provision of these payments with a view to assisting western grain producers. What my hon. friend has been saying is a far cry indeed from the subject of aid to western grain producers.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Chair feels that it has been lenient with the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. I am sure he will try to abide by the thoughts of the Chair and stick to item 698.

I have not discussed one matter in my remarks today that was not
[The Deputy Chairman.]

under debate on the supplementary item on September 6 of which this is merely an extension or when the item was explained by the Prime Minister on August 30. This is an item that is based on need and the point I am endeavouring to make is that it is not satisfactory. It was admitted to be a stopgap, a temporary measure, and I think we should hear from the administration whether or not during this session we are going to get another proposal in substitution for this at the expiry of its first year that will be more in keeping with the expectations of the farmers as a result of the former policies of the Prime Minister and as a result of the need in western Canada particularly because of rising costs and inflation that is still unchecked.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks on this item at this time. I have listened with a great deal of interest to the speech of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. While I am not going to try to cover the ground he covered because I do not want to get the same reception from the Chair, I do wish to say that as far as western Canada is concerned this item, as a general solution to the problem faced by the farmers of that area, is in their opinion entirely inadequate. The dollar per acre, which we are discussing at this time as a supplementary payment, means very little today in relation to the budget of the agriculture producer and the costs that he must assume.
The reaction to this policy, in general, has been one of disappointment; it has been one of great concern because the producers have felt that this policy of one dollar per acre for one year is completely inadequate and does not constitute the fulfilment of the government's agricultural program as they have understood it. A dollar per acre related to the average yield is a very small sum of money. If it is related to the crop yield only on an acre it would be about five cents per bushel. One would have to relate it, of course, to the fact that it is paid on all acres and it could be, therefore, between 10 cents and 15 cents a bushel.
How about relating it to domestic consumption in Canada?

When the farmer hauls his grain to the elevator he does not divide his load between domestic consumption and export. He is interested in the price he gets, although he would be interested if, in paying for this grain, the government would adopt a policy of dividing the payment and by that means providing the farmer with a larger payment.

Another reason the farmers feel that this is most unsatisfactory is that it is a temporary measure. It is a one-year measure; it is a one-shot affair. I think, perhaps, I heard those words this afternoon, and I think I used them myself many months ago. This is a policy that has brought great disappointment to the producers of western Canada. This is the reason the western farmers are coming to Ottawa in a mass delegation within a few weeks. I noticed the applause from the government benches, and that is the best response that this mass delegation has yet received from those benches. When this delegation was first mentioned in this house, I was accused of having organized it.
You tried it.

The Prime Minister said to me, "You hoped to bring a lot of western farmers who would march on Ottawa, but you came alone." I came all alone, so far as the opposition is concerned, as has been pointed out very effectively this afternoon. We have had contributions ranging from gold to international trade made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, while dealing with the policy of parity prices and deficiency payments-I apparently came all alone.
There are a great many farmers coming to Ottawa and a general representation of the people of Saskatchewan by occupational groups, according to press reports that we all read, within a matter of some weeks. I congratulate the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River for the versatility he has shown in this house, and for repairing what was a very serious omission, I believe, in a speech made by the Leader of the Opposition. It was a very interesting and very enjoyable speech, a speech that I thought was more effective than similar speeches on other occasions. The omission to which I refer is the lack of any substantial reference to the problem now under discussion.
Do not forget his speech of September 6.

But the Leader of the Opposition did not say where the Liberal party stood. Of course, that was in keeping with the general attitude of the official opposition. We ask the government its policy; we tear down the government, but divulge our policy-never. As I was saying, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is the only member, and he can correct me if I am wrong, who runs on a Liberal-Labour ticket. Now, of course, he is going to take on a third dimension because he is taking in agriculture.

We have some good
farmers in northern Ontario.
Supp ly-A griculture

He is the financial critic of the opposition, so we are most interested in the statement he has made.
The reason the producers are dissatisfied with the dollar per acre under consideration is that, with this and everything else the government is doing, the agricultural producers are painfully aware that the prices they receive today in terms of purchasing power are lower than at any time in the history of this country with the exception of three years in the thirties when we had the R. B. Bennett government. We are hopeful that the government may yet change its attitude; that they will consider the matter of deficiency payments for western grain, and adopt a policy which the Minister of Agriculture has incorporated in the Agricultural Prices Support Act, a technique that has not yet been used in the sale of grain under the Department of Trade and Commerce.
I do not feel that the deficiency payment technique that has been used so far is adequate. There is one detail concerning the application of this measure about which I should like to ask the minister. Payments are made in general, I think perhaps exclusively, on the basis of the acreage listed in the permit book held by the wheat board. I have found, and I was surprised at this, a great many farmers who are unable to qualify for assistance under this measure because they do not have a permit book. They are farmers who produce grain but who feed their grain to livestock. I do not know how many would be involved, but I would think several thousands in western Canada would be involved.
Wrong again.

I would think this would be particularly true in the province of Manitoba, and it is certainly true in areas that are being developed where the farms are small, quarter section or bush farms, so-called-
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Is he aware that was rectified? It was a regulation of the Canadian wheat board and the commissioners of the wheat board knew nothing about it. Most of these farmers are now receiving permit books.

I am pleased to have contributions from all sides of the house. If the minister confirms that fact, I shall be pleased because I think it is a serious omission. I think these people are bona fide farmers and are entitled to this dollar payment.

Supply-Agriculture
I would be most happy if it applied to all farmers on an equal basis, so that every person would be entitled to receive payments because he has a cultivated acreage. If that is being done, as I say, it is most welcome and it probably accounts for a substantial part of the supplementary estimate under consideration.

As a point of order, Mr. Chairman, do I understand that you have ruled we are not, under this item, permitted to discuss the adequacy or inadequacy of this particular proposal, which inevitably involves us in a discussion of the government's support price program and whether or not the government's general assurances, at other times, have been fulfilled? Do I take it that is your position?
Before you reply, may I say with great respect that you would want to consider the situation which prevailed in this house when this item was discussed on September 6 last. I must point out to Your Honour that sitting in the chair which you now occupy at that time was the chairman of committees.
The item before the house was precisely in the wording which now confront us. On that occasion the Prime Minister spoke. If you will examine what he said when speaking to this very item as part of the principal estimate at that time, it will be found that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River certainly was in order if the Prime Minister on that occasion was in order. The Prime Minister on that occasion, in discussing this particular policy, referred to old age pensions, unemployment insurance and his own election promises. He dealt with the over-all policy of the government in the matter of agriculture. Since that day the house has not had an opportunity of taking up the discussion from where the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Assiniboia left off.
In effect, Mr. Chairman, what you have said to those of us in this group who are seeking to examine the government's agriculture policy as a whole, is this: "It is true that the Prime Minister had this opportunity; it is true that the hon. member for Assiniboia had it; but you in this particular group are to be denied it because parliament prorogued just at the end of that particular discussion." I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that this rule does not lend itself to the restrictive interpretation that you have given it. I suggest that on this item we should be allowed to examine whether or not this proposal meets the need of the farmers in western Canada and whether it is in fulfilment of assurances given by the administration to these farmers. That examination will involve a discussion as to whether or not there are
available other solutions-some promised,, some offered on the side-to meet with a situation which undoubtedly has provoked the anger of farmers all over western Canada.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, may I say first of all that the last remark of the hon. member in speaking to the point of order was completely out of order and also was completely incorrect. The statement made by the hon. member for Essex East that everything concerning agriculture should be discussed on this item is, in my opinion, manifestly not correct. This is only one item amongst scores of items with regard to the agriculture estimates. To attempt to say that price supports are an integral part of this discussion is complete nonsense. Price supports have nothing to do with this payment at all and have absolutely no relevancy to it.

We did not say
that.
The hon. member for Essex East did say that. He said that price supports were definitely connected with this matter and that it should be possible to discuss them in dealing with this item.
As alternative policies; certainly.
As far as the Prime Minister was concerned, I think the hon. member will find that the Prime Minister did not make his statement in connection with this matter.
Yes; he did.
Not on this item. If my memory serves me correctly, I think it will be found that the Prime Minister made his statement on motions.
If I might correct the minister may I say that he made it in both places.
He made it first on motions. In any event the general statement in regard to the matter was made on motions and not on this particular item.
He covered four pages of Hansard.

This general contention of the hon. member for Essex East and, before him by practice, by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, that under this item we should be able to discuss any matter concerning agriculture is, in my opinion, just not reasonable in view of the fact that, as I say, there are scores of items with regard to agriculture in the regular estimates; and it is manifestly unreasonable to try to discuss all these things in a supplementary estimate of this kind.

On the point of order,
Mr. Chairman, may I say this. If you will look at page 4738 of Hansard of September 6, 1958, you will find an item in exactly the same terms as the item that we have before us in the supplementary estimates at this time. On that page and the following two or three pages, Mr. Chairman, you will find a record of the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture and in which he discussed, among other things, price supports. Then a little bit later on you will find a record of a long statement made by the Prime Minister in which he discussed a great many things. Indeed, he went so far that, as reported at page 4753, the hon. member for Assiniboia referred to the Prime Minister's dragging in everything but the kitchen sink. That discussion on that occasion in respect of an item exactly similar to this one was allowed to range over the whole field of agriculture in so far as it affected the item. I assume that you, Mr. Chairman, would want to take now exactly the same stand as you took then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is one observation I should like to make on the point of order, if I may. We are here dealing with a supplementary estimate.
We were doing so then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The position is quite different. There we were dealing with a new item introduced into the estimates. It is true that they were supplementary estimates but it was a new item. Here what you have before you is an item that calls for an additional sum for the same purpose. The question before the committee on this item, I therefore take it, is whether this additional sum should be voted for this particular purpose. As the explanatory notes indicate, the purpose of this bill is to enact that every cheque, draft, traveller's cheque, bill of exchange, postal note, money order, postal remittance and any other similar remittance of any department as defined in paragraph (f) of section 2 of the Financial Administration Act or of any crown corporation enumerated in schedules B, C and D of the said act, shall be printed in both the English and the French languages.
Last year, even more than this year, we noted among all hon. members a desire for greater understanding of the provisions of the British North America Act and what it involves, namely the use of both official languages in Canada.
In fact, ever since I have been sitting in this house, I have been amazed at the extensive use being made of French to express opinions. I wish to commend all members, and particularly those who, though they may be only learning to express themselves in French, are making efforts that we, Frenchspeaking members, appreciate and admire.
This explains why the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) promptly saw to it that speeches made in the House of Commons be simultaneously translated, so that members of either language may follow proceedings without having to wait for the official translation which is published the following day in Hansard.
Certain members may find it odd that after 90 years under a federal system which places the French and English languages on an equal footing in Canada, it should be necessary to introduce in this house a bill designed to give official recognition to a principle contained in the very constitution of this country.
The present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), whose worthy efforts to learn French I heartily commend, will certainly agree with his predecessors in the high office he holds in the cabinet, that, from a technical point of view, absolutely nothing forbids the printing in both languages of federal government cheques and other negotiable instruments. The technical difficulties are no greater than those involved in printing bilingual money or postage stamps which proclaim to the face of the world that Canada is a country basically made up of two great races, living in harmony and mutual respect.
I know that, by virtue of the authority he holds within the treasury board, the Minister of Finance could request that federal


government cheques and other negotiable instruments be printed in both languages, as are family allowance cheques issued to residents of Quebec, cheques issued by certain other federal services, and many official federal documents.
The bill I am introducing would, in fact, be pointless if its main purpose were not to reiterate to the Minister of Finance and to all the members of the cabinet the will that was clearly expressed in this house during the last session of the 23rd parliament, when a bill similar in every respect received a practically unanimous vote.
I do not expect that any member will feel it necessary to express his views about an obvious matter, even if the house has undergone certain changes at this session. That is why I am convinced that my Conservative friends, as well as the members of the C.C.F. party, and even the Liberals, will feel it desirable to reiterate without delay the unanimous will of the house on the matter now before the house.
Right-minded English Canadians are showing great regard for the French language and it can be said that culture-loving people learn this language. This is why, in 1957, we have heard our gracious Queen give a flawless reading of the French version of the speech from the throne. Again last year, the Prime Minister of Great Britain, the Right Hon. Harold Macmillan, used perfect French in the address he gave to this House of Commons.
Quite recently, a professor at the university of Western Ontario expressed the hope that both official languages would be used equally in all ten provinces, and he added:
-according to legislation, Canada is a bilingual country, even though the law finds its application only in the official documents of the federal government and in the province of Quebec.
That same professor suggested that French be taught to all school children 8 to 9 years old, and, he said:
*-where it is done, this teaching is successful.
In the same line, Dr. Jeanneret, pioneer of the teaching of French in Ontario, suggested the same thing and, after the adoption of the resolution by the Canadian Conference on Education, he added:
-that the teaching of a secondary language should be practised from coast to coast, in public and secondary schools, French being taught in the English provinces and English in the province of Quebec.
And so, he went on to say:
-the same harmony, the same spirit of "live and let live" between English-speaking Canadians and

French-speaking Canadians, would prevail as they do between English, Scottish and Irish Canadians.
If the views expressed by those educators were put into practice, the government would find that the whole nation would welcome an official decision which would implement the people's will, so clearly expressed through their representatives. I know that two of my Conservative colleagues, the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm and the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Messrs. Pigeon and Ricard) have put on the order paper a bill for similar purpose.
I therefore call on their co-operation not to delay the debate and prevent the second reading of this bill, before the house takes recess. Any delay caused by their colleagues on the government side would create the impression that they cannot count on those colleagues' co-operation in having this bill passed when their own bills are submitted to the house in the near future.
I therefore urge the movers of these bills to use their influence on their Conservative colleagues to have the question put immediately.

This question has come before the house on previous occasions. Those of us who were elected as recently as I was and as some of my colleagues were on June 10, 1957, recall some very interesting debates concerning this legislation that took place during the session after that election. But the subject has been discussed on numerous occasions prior to that and one's knowledge of the subject is enriched very considerably if he avails himself of the opportunity to study the debates and some of the very learned contributions that were made to the discussions of the subject by some of the distinguished hon. members who participated in the debates on those occasions.
One question that has not been raised by the hon. member who moved this bill but which was raised by an hon. gentleman during the session held between 1957 and 1958 concerns whether or not there is a need for legislation of this kind; in other words, whether or not the legislation in its present form would authorize the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) to direct that cheques of the kind contemplated by the proposed legislation be printed in both languages without any resort to new legislation at all.
As a matter of fact, the present Minister of Finance was questioned about this possibility in this house in December of 1957. The minister then quite frankly stated to the house that this was a matter as to which a legal opinion would have to be obtained and given. It may be, then, that if no legislation is needed the debate that takes place on the proposed bill of the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) is academic.
Certainly as I understand the practice and from what I have been able to observe in the study I have given the subject, in the province of Quebec cheques of the kind referred to in the proposed legislation are already printed and distributed in the French language and unless there has been some recent change I have also discovered that some of the cheques distributed on behalf of the St. Lawrence seaway authority and by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are likewise printed in the French language.

It was a Conservative administration that in the year 1934 enacted legislation whereby currency was printed in French. Two other similar bills are on the order paper which would have the effect of introducing bilingualism into the field of cheques. These bills have been introduced by two members of our party, the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) and the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). Both have private member's bills on the order paper whose objective is similar to that of the bill we are now discussing.
