Another fact that indicates the thinking of hon. members of the house is the effort of so many of them to learn the French or English language, depending on the language of their origin. I think immediately of the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Walker) and the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Stinson) whom I have heard address the house on previous occasions in the French language. While I do not recall him having addressed the house in the French language, I also know something of the efforts of the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Small) to study and learn the French language. These to


me are evidences of a desire on the part of hon. members, certainly on our side of the house, to develop a knowledge and understanding of the French language that will enable them to speak fluently in that tongue,
Opposition to this legislation comes from different quarters. It is not bounded by party or by race. For example, if you will look at the debates in 1956 you will find that the then minister of finance, Mr. Harris, in what was obviously an effort to put a stop to a debate on this very subject on a private member's bill, got up on a point of order and said that it was out of order for a private member to introduce this kind of legislation because it involved the expenditure of public money. When he attempted to develop on what basis the expenditure of public money was involved he said that it was because it would cost more to print cheques in the French language. But quite happily his point of order did not get very far.
I only bring that to the attention of the house for the purpose of showing that this is a subject on which there has always been controversy and opposite views are expressed and have been historically by members on our side of the house and by men like the former minister of finance, Mr. Harris, a member of the party now on the opposite side of the house.
There is certainly nothing to fear from this kind of legislation. If you trace the history of comparable legislation you will find that in 1927 postal orders, money orders and excise stamps were all made bilingual. In 1934, as I have already mentioned, we had the first experiment with the use of currency in the French language. I recall that it was in 1936 that bilingual currency as we now know it was first implemented.
All of these things have not tended to disunite us. If anything, they have promoted unity. The circulation of such items throughout the various provinces of our country has fostered unity rather than set it back and so, in my opinon, will cheques which have become such a widely used medium by means of which the government transacts its business. It will not only tend to further the advance of unity at home but, as one member put it in the debate in 1957, it proclaims abroad our bi-ethnical character. It is simply a further extension of a principle that is already fully recognized and has been traditional over the years.
The hon. member who moved second reading of the bill commented upon the fact that so many visitors who come to Ottawa

Indeed, all the officials of other lands who come to this country expect, by reason of their knowledge of what is really meant by Canadianism, that that is the thing to do when they come here, and as far as I am concerned that is very desirable and commendable. I am pleased to have had the opportunity to speak to the house. I am pleased to have had the opportunity to speak in support of the principle put forward by the hon. member who has moved second reading of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, this is my first opportunity to address the house during this session. It is no easy task to address the house just after we have heard so brilliant a speech as the one just made by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Maloney). Undoubtedly he dealt exhaustively with the matter and there is not much more to be said. Nevertheless I would like to express my own views in the matter.
Of course, Bill No. C-4 introduced today by the hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska (Mr. Boulanger), is not new to hon. members. Its history was given a moment ago and it indicates that this matter has come up on several occasions. Before discussing the matter in detail, I must say that as a French Canadian living in the province of Quebec, and simply as a Canadian, I am in favour of the principle of the bill. But, as the hon. member for Parkdale indicated a moment ago, the constitution already provides for the use of the French and English languages in the country and, consequently, I do not think it should be necessary to adopt special legislation to that effect. If you refer back to the act of confederation, the British North America Act of 1867, which, by the way, is the work of great Conservatives like Macdonald and Cartier, you will realize that Section 133 clearly states the rights of the French language and of the English language. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will read into the record those sections so often referred to, which are known to many people but which others may not be familiar with. I quote:
133. Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the Houses of the Parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec; and both those
Financial Administration Act languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this act, and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
The acts of the Parliament of Canada and of the legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
It seems evident to me that the rights of the French language were protected from the time of the adoption of the new constitution in 1867 and that the fathers of confederation had had this very matter in mind. Anyway, the Conservative party has always protected the rights of real Canadianism, and has always endeavoured to foster national unity in the country. I am sure the Conservative party will keep working for the continued advancement of Confederation which they established in Canada, and whose centennial it will be our pleasure to celebrate a few years hence. While French Canada has its own beliefs and traditions, its contribution to Canadian culture has been a very important one for the whole country. So important was it, Mr. Speaker, and this is worth pointing out-that it prevented the absorption of our country by our powerful neighbours to the south. Long before Alaska, Canada would have become the 49th state. I believe that the French-Canadian culture, joined to the English culture, has helped us to safeguard our country's independence, because the Americans were in the process of assimilating the whole of North America. French Canadians-nobody will dispute this -are an asset to the Canadian nation and a natural barrier against American assimilation.
The Bank of Canada Act is quite clear about the printing of government's negotiable instruments, because under subsection (3) of section 20, chapter 13 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, Canadian government cheques are payable or negotiable at par. Nothing at all prescribes that they be printed solely in English. Besides, subsection 1 of section 21 gives to the Bank of Canada the exclusive right to issue bank notes.
Consequently, I believe that, in this matter, French Canadians and English Canadians are of one mind. In any case, it is provided for in the Canadian constitution. Last year, in this house, our Prime Minister expressed surprise that this right had been disputed, for, according to the constitution, it would be normal that all government instruments be printed in both languages, since our constitution guarantees the use of both French and English.

With all due regard tor my good friend the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska, and I congratulate him on having introduced this bill, thereby giving us a chance to go into this matter-I say that, if we had to vote on the question, I would prefer, in my humble opinion, to consider bill number C-9, introduced by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), because it is more comprehensive and includes, in a more specific way, all negotiable instruments that would have to be printed in both official languages. As pointed out by the previous speaker, the Conservative government has already granted simultaneous translation. The former government had done a great deal of talking about it; many times, it had been asked to establish this system, but never did. That is why I have no doubt that the Conservative government will take the necessary steps to grant bilingual cheques from one end of the country to the other.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PRINTING OF NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS IN BOTH ENGLISH AND FRENCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to take part in this debate concerning the printing of negotiable government documents in both the English and French languages. The previous occasion when this bill was brought before us was in the dying days of the 23rd session of parliament. It was brought forward for our attention on the Friday before the house prorogued, when we had very little time to discuss the issue, and the vote was sprung on us very quickly. As the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Maloney) said we, as politicians as he preferred to call us, have a duty to be frank in our thinking and in our discussions. I think if that were not the case, we would not be here.
This is a subject of great national importance and of national interest. It is an extremely controversial subject. At the outset, Mr. Speaker and members of the house, let me make it clear that I fully appreciate the thought that lies behind the British North America Act. I appreciate also the fact that these two races are living side by side in Canada and that they have managed to get along well. I am very proud to be a member of this party which, as was said a few minutes ago, was instrumental in having the money of our country printed in both languages. I am proud also of the fact that it was the Conservative party that installed the simultaneous translation system. Personally, I have found it to be of great help in following the debates that have taken place in this honoured house. I think, in addition, it has done much to maintain the attendance of the house and to arouse interest in all the debates that have occurred in French or English.
I appreciate also the fact that this bill refers to government documents only. The remarks I have to make, which may express a view contrary to some of the views already expressed, will certainly not be uttered in any spirit of animosity whatever. I assure my French-speaking friends in this house and outside of it that my thinking in this matter will be in no way whatsoever a reflection on their nationality. I would think that this bill is a matter that we should discuss carefully. I think we should give it a good hearing. As I have said before, and as one of the hon. members who has spoken has said, this is an extremely controversial subject. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps we should make haste slowly on this subject or that, as has been said, perhaps we should count to ten before we proceed. At this stage I am

wondering just how great is the importance of this bill at this present time when this country is confronted with great international problems. I refer to the race for supremacy of the air, in the days of the sputniks, and getting control of the orbits; our great problems of international trade; the economic war confronting us at this particular time; and all those matters which are of such great importance. I am wondering, Mr. Speaker, whether we should not be spending our time on such matters as these. I am wondering whether we should not be debating a subject which is perhaps more important just at the present time.

speechtext:
Do not misunderstand me, Mr. Speaker. The matter has importance, but having regard to the order of importance, I would think that there are others that should come first. At this particular time I think we should be thinking of the curtailment of government expenditures. Many of us were elected on the platform that we would watch government expenditures and would curtail them. By putting into force a bill such as this one and having all government negotiable documents printed bilingually, of necessity some expense will be incurred. Some may say that it is only trivial. It is only a small point but these small points add up to big totals. I still say it would be an added expense at this particular time.
I believe this bill is designed to extend the use of bilingualism and that it goes beyond the provisions of the British North America Act. If this attitude were adopted by ethnic groups, the result might well be multilingualism rather than bilingualism. What about all these other groups in our country who have their native tongues? Perhaps some of them would like to see cheques and government documents printed in their language. I think we must stop and consider this point with respect to its ultimate results. I would ask myself and hon. members of this house these questions: Is there a real need for this bill at the present time? What hardships, if any, are being created by the lack of bilingualism on any of the government money documents? What about people in the areas of Canada where French is spoken by a fairly high percentage? Is there any great suffering occurring among these people? How many folks, say in Quebec, would hand out a $10 bill for a dollar bill, or vice versa? I believe it has been stated here that the cheques of the C.B.C., and the seaway corporation and possibly the baby bonus cheques
Supply-Agriculture
are now printed bilingually. If this is the case, I cannot see the need for this bill at the present time.
As to these cheques to which reference is being made, even although they are printed in only one language, namely the English language, the figures appear as 10, 20, 30 or 40, whatever the amount may be; and those figures are the same in English or in French. I therefore do not think there is any great hardship on anybody with respect to these cheques being printed only in the English language.
I would suggest to my hon. friends and to the house that we should weigh this matter in the true light of its necessity at this particular time. I would think that the hon. member who introduced this bill would have been accomplishing something that met a greater need or would be of greater use to this country at this particular time if he had introduced a bill, as I intend to do at some later date, to provide that all cheques be of a standard size and that they will be standard in their printing. The name of the bank issuing them and the amount will appear in a certain place. The signature and everything about that cheque will be uniform. No matter where you go in Canada the size, the printing and everything about the cheque will be uniform. For those in business and those in banks who are obliged to handle thousands of cheques each day, this fact of having uniform cheques would, in my opinion, be the first step in this direction.

It being 6 o'clock, the house will resume consideration of the business which was interrupted at 5 o'clock.

The house resumed in committee of supply, Mr. McGee in the chair.

698. To provide for payments to western grain producers of $1 per acre up to a maximum of 200 acres per farm in accordance with regulations of the governor in council-further amount required, $1,300,000.

Supply-Agriculture
The Acling Chairman (Mr. McGee): It being 6 o'clock I do now leave the chair.
At 6 o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, we were discussing the matter of the dollar an acre payment up to a maximum of $200 covered by the vote now before the committee and before our consideration of this question was interrupted at five o'clock a request was made to me to explain why this increased amount of money was required. In addition, some complaint was made by one or two hon. members of the Liberal party, I believe, that I had not given an explanation of this matter.
The committee will recall that when this vote was originally passed last session it provided for $40 million out of which these payments would be made. On the basis of the number of permit books which had been issued in previous years it was estimated that $40 million would be ample to cover these payments. However, once the announcement had been made that the payments were to be disbursed the wheat board, which had been designated as the agent of the Minister of Agriculture for the purpose of making these payments, began to receive a large number of applications for permit books, in some cases from people who had had permit books in previous years but who had not applied for them in the 1957-58 crop year, and in other cases from people who had never had a permit book previously.
There were some 4,000 applications, as I recall the figures, from people who had had permit books before. The acreages which they claimed could, of course, be checked against the acreage recorded in their previous permit books. There were a further 4,000 applications from people who had not had a permit book before, and in these cases there was no means of checking whether the acreage claimed was, in fact, the acreage which these farmers held. In these circumstances some other means had to be taken to check these claims. Payments were, however, made as rapidly as possible to the farmers whose claims could be readily authenticated, and by November 24 a total of 214,194 payments had been made to a total value of $37,712,156. This completed the main body of the 1958-59 permits which had been issued and processed by the wheat board to that date.
The wheat board proceeded to make all the investigations it could into the other cases,

and the Department of Agriculture also made investigations with regard to the further applications which were pending for permit books, and as at January 29 payments had been made to a total value of $39,887,459 to 227,919 permit book holders. The average value of the cheques issued was $175.
How many acres?

I have not got the number of acres, but the sum covers that number of permit holders. At the present time the wheat board is in the course of processing some 6,000 further applications and it is expected that an additional 2,000 applications will be received before the end of the crop year. As new permits are issued acreage payments will be made to the permit holders. On the basis of the average amount paid out so far we calculate that these extra permits will necessitate the payment of an additional $1,300,000. That is the amount of this present vote, and that is the reason why the money is being asked.
I should now like to say a few words in connection with some of the statements which have been made in the course of the discussion so far. The hon. member for Assiniboia says that the reaction to this scheme was one of disappointment and concern. An opinion along the same lines was indicated by the hon. member for Essex East and by certain hon. members. The figures which I have just given, figures which indicate that a very large number of people who did not have them before have now applied for permit books, indicate that these people, at least, were not disappointed. On the other hand they seem to have been delighted.
I have received more letters in connection with this subject than anyone else in Canada, I should think, and I must say that the reaction I have noted is not the reaction indicated by the hon. member for Assiniboia and by other hon. members opposite. The great majority of the people who have written to me about this are extremely pleased to get these payments, and tell me how much the payments will help them. The only difficulty expressed is by people who have not yet been able to get a permit book or who have not yet received their payments and are wondering why it has not been sent. My impression that this scheme has been very well received has been confirmed by the many conversations I have had with farmers in the west and by my experiences in addressing the conventions of the Manitoba farmers' union, the Saskatchewan farmers' union and the Alberta farmers' union.
Naturally, everybody in this country- farmers, trade unionists, manufacturers and

so forth-asks for more. If a manufacturer wants us to increase a tariff and it is by any chance increased, he wants us to increase it a little more, and the same applies with regard to everyone else in this country no matter to what section of the community he belongs. It is only natural that the farmers would like more. That is human nature, and it is to be expected. However, the general reaction which I have received-and I think this will be confirmed by a large number of other members in the house-is that this scheme has been received with considerable gratification on account of the payments which have been made.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River said this measure was strictly for the benefit of the people of western Canada. I should like to take issue with him with regard to that statement. These payments have been of great benefit to people all over Canada. They have resulted, and will result, in a great deal of employment in manufacturing communities in the central part of this country, and the general benefits which will flow from this $40 million are by no means confined to western Canada. They will be spread all over Canada and have an important effect on maintaining employment and on sustaining the general economy.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River also talked as if this $40 million was all the money which had been devoted to agriculture during the past year. Nothing could be further from the truth. I recommend the hon. gentleman to read the speech I made in this chamber on January 23, because he will find in that speech some indication of the very large number of things which this government has done for agriculture during the past year, including reference to the fact that well over $165 million was paid out in direct payments to assist agriculture, and that in addition at least $100 million was added to the income of dairy farmers through the operation of the stabilization board, money which these farmers would never have received had it not been for the operation of the board under the appropriate legislation.
I should like, further, to point out to the hon. member that last year was the best year that farmers have experienced since 1952. Their cash income was 10 per cent above that of the previous year, and 20 per cent above that of 1955 or for 1954. At the same time the increase in the cost of the goods and services which farmers have to buy went up by just over 1 per cent.

In one year?

Yes, in one year. As I say, this is the first time since 1952 that the cost-price squeeze of which we have heard so much in this chamber has been finally halted and reversed.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I may ask the minister a question.
Certainly.
Would the minister say the halting of the cost-price squeeze also applied to grain producers and to the price of grain?

Yes, it applied to the grain producers. They received 6 per cent more by way of cash last year than they did the year before. I believe that is all I should say at this moment in connection with this matter. I feel that I have explained why the extra $1,300,000 is required and I trust that the committee will see fit to agree to this vote.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to embarrass the Chair by departing at all from the speeches made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture in introducing the original item of $40 million to which they are now asking us to add $1,300,000. I am going to follow very closely certain statements that were made, the first made by the Prime Minister on August 30, 1958, and the second made by the Minister of Agriculture on September 6, 1958, with reference to this particular item.
I may say, sir, that the approach I am making to this item is this. The present government asked the house to vote $40 million out of the treasury and the taxes of everybody in Canada from coast to coast for this purpose. We acceded to the government's request without dissent from the house. We are now being asked to vote an additional sum of $1,300,000. It seems to me that it ill becomes the members of the treasury benches who are responsible to this house to question our right to examine whether the claims they made when they introduced this policy have in fact been carried out and it is some of those claims that I now propose to examine somewhat analytically.
I wish first to refer to a statement made by the Prime Minister on August 30, 1958. For convenience I am using the unrevised edition of Hansard and I would refer hon. members to the words of the Prime Minister in a statement made on Saturday, August 30.

of grain, we are being asked at this time to add another $1,300,000. I have no doubt that perhaps the Prime Minister was more accurate last August than on this later occasion. But I do say that to ask members of the house from every part of Canada to make an addition to this vote on the basis of need, which was the basis put forward by the Minister of Agriculture, in my view makes it incumbent upon the government to meet other and similar needs in other and similar industries and regions, as the Prime Minister indicated was the intention of the government, an intention about which we have heard no more since August 30 last. I do say, even though in this free parliament it apparently is wrong to say anything about fishermen, that I hope the Prime Minister will remember that principle with which he announced this policy.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take part in this discussion and express the approval of some 8,000 prairie farmers to the Minister of Agriculture and the government for the $1 an acre supplementary benefit paid last year. I should like to say that when our friends on this side of the house who sit immediately in front of me treat this matter in the airy, fairy-like manner in which they have today they should know why they are sitting where they are, and they will sit there for a long time.
The hon. member for Assiniboia expressed the disappointment of all farmers. I spent four months talking to some 8,000 farmers who expressed complete approbation. I suggest to the hon. member for Assiniboia that he should visit individual farmers in his constituency instead of discussing these matters with heads of organizations who perhaps are not quite as close to the grass as the hon. member should be.
In my constituency there are some 15,000 homes and over 8,000 of them or 60 per cent are occupied by farmers. The other 40 per cent depend entirely on the earnings of the farmers in the constituency, and last year the $1 an acre provided very substantial and real help at a time when ready money was most welcome to anybody and particularly to the farmers who had nothing but a lot of promises for many years. Sixty per cent of the farmers in my constituency farm 240 acres or less and market no grain

Supply-Agriculture
although they do have seeded acreage. Fifteen per cent farm 320 acres and market approximately 500 bushels annually. Ten per cent whose farms are a little larger market between 500 and 1,000 bushels. Ten per cent market between 1,000 and 2,000 bushels and five per cent market over 2,000 bushels annually. The bonus of $1 an acre paid last year gave the farmers in my constituency approximately $800,000 and in a constituency of small farms that is a very substantial help not only to the farmers themselves but also to the merchants, lawyers, doctors, dentists, machinery agents, car salesmen and thus to all Canada.
The reason that the farmers in my constituency do not market too much grain, although they are genuine farmers, lies in the fact that in 1958 approximately 100,000 head of beef cattle and 350,000 head of hogs were marketed from the constituency. We have a large dairy industry which supports-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Shall we come back to grain?

I am trying to relate how my constituency was affected by the payment of this $1 an acre and I think I am doing fairly well. We have had quite a discussion today of the relative merit of deficiency payments vis-a-vis the payment of $1 an acre, as well as discussion of other extraneous matters. However, so far as my constituency is concerned, about 15 per cent of the farmers would benefit by deficiency payments and 100 per cent will benefit by the payment of the $1 per acre.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, may I congratulate the Department of Trade and Commerce upon a news item I read today which stated that they had marketed 5.5 million bushels of wheat and 3.7 million bushels of barley to the government of Poland.

In rising to speak on this item, I should like to congratulate the government upon the help they have given to the western farmer. A few minutes ago I listened to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate giving a real Liberal speech in which he begrudged the western farmers the few dollars they have been given over the last period of months. The Liberals see the results of that attitude today.
We did not bring this dollar an acre payment in as a cure-all. We brought it in to fill the gap until we could get the long range agricultural policy into operation. This $200 that the farmers received last fall meant a great deal to all the farmers in my constituency. I spoke to one merchant who said it was one of the best things we had ever

done. It had brought business into the town to the extent of $1,200 in that particular day.
The only real kick one hears about this $200 payment to the farmers is from the C.C.F. party. They seem to be worried about it. They are very much afraid we are going to do something for the farmers, and they will be left out in the cold. According to the Edmonton Journal, the leader of the C.C.F. party made the remark that he had not found one farmer who was in favour of this $200. If the hon. member would come to my constituency, and I had the time I would drive him around and introduce him to a few. However, he spends too much time elsewhere.
Mention was made of the fact that the farmers were going to march on Ottawa because they had only received this $200, but that is not the case. We have always received delegations in Ottawa, and we always will. When you try to connect this mass delegation with this $200 payment you find there is just no connection. If the hon. member for Assini-boia was not so busy trying to form this mass delegation and would pay attention to his constituents I do not think he would have this idea. I can assure them that if they come to Ottawa we will receive them with courtesy.

After the Newfoundland fishermen had a difficult time in swimming in our seas, perhaps the representative of an industrial riding ought to express his opinion of the vote that is now before us. I intend to support the request of the minister for an additional $1,300,000 to pay the farmers this $1 per acre. However, at the same time, we realize that this payment is not based on any principle at all. It is a handout, pure and simple.
The people of Canada are becoming increasingly worried about the demands upon governments for handouts. We have them for the shipbuilding industry; we have been asked to supply them for shipping on the great lakes; we have them for the mining enterprises of Canada, the manufacturers of Canada, and the coal industry has had them for some years. Mention has been made recently of the fact we will have to give some subsidies to Canadian railways as well. There are a great number of taxpayers who are beginning to wonder where this policy of paying subsidies is going to end. If it were not for our knowledge of the needs of western farmers for this money we would take a very close look at this whole proposition.
It is not based on any principle at all. No one has yet explained why the sum of $1 per acre is to be paid. Why not pay $5 per acre or why not pay 50 cents per acre? No one has explained why the farmer is limited

to a maximum of 200 acres on which he can collect payments. No one has yet explained what is going to be done in the year 1959. Are we going to be asked to vote a similar amount or a larger amount? Is this business of paying a subsidy, a handout, going to become an evil that is so rooted in our national way of life that we cannot get down to equity for all the working people of Canada?
The people of my riding have long realized that the farmers do not want handouts. The farmers want parity, and the people of my riding are highly organized workers, so they realize the value of organized workers bargaining across the table. They feel that agriculture ought to have some right to sit across the table and bargain, lay down the facts and figures, and obtain a fair deal. This is nothing of the sort. This is charity and not parity. This does not apply to the whole of Canadian agriculture. It applies to only a limited section of Canadian agriculture, and it is to be regretted on that point alone. We believe that the subsidy has to be paid this time. However, we would ask this government, if it does not want to find other sections of Canada beginning to complain to base their subsidies on a principle that can be defended to the fishermen in Newfoundland and to the old age pensioner in Burnaby as well.
We feel it is high time that the government attempted to estimate the basic needs of Canadian agriculture, and not resort to methods of this type. This will in no way resolve the basic problems of Canadian agriculture. It will only mean a little relief to one section of Canadian agriculture. I feel that the Canadian farmers, even the western farmers, have every right to organize a march on Ottawa because certainly they had no reason before March 31 last to believe that what they would be offered would be a handout. They had every reason to believe that the new government which they were electing was going to attend to the fundamental problems.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I believe the hon. member is quite far away from the question being debated at the moment. I must ask him to confine his remarks to this item No. 698.

After listening to the remarks which I heard first from speakers on the opposition side, I am reminded of a story that has been attributed to the senior senator from Illinois, Senator Douglas. After hearing an argument, equally prolix and irrelevant, he said it reminded him of his grandmother's hoopskirt; it covered everything and touched nothing.
Mr. Chairman, from the intellectual gymnastics we have observed and the flow of
Supply-Agriculture
words we have heard it seems to me that the views of the opposition-and I include both the official opposition and the members of the C.C.F. group-are that they are opposed to this particular measure. I may be wrong in drawing that inference. If so, I hope that before this discussion concludes they will stand up and admit that is not the case or that they may have been converted by the arguments of the minister and the members of the Conservative party. However, as I say, that seems to me to be the impression to be taken from their remarks. I am sure it will make most interesting reading to the farmers in western Canada.
The hon. member was not listening.

I observe from the speech of the Minister of Agriculture on September 6, 1958 that the principle on which these payments were made is a simple one. It is set out at page 4739 of Hansard as follows:
The principle upon which these payments are based is to extend the greatest amount of assistance to those who need it most, that is, to the small farmers. That is the basic principle underlying this type of payment and, of course, there is a definite formula.
I come from a constituency in which there are a great number of small farmers. I have personally observed the effect these payments have had on their financial situation, their ability to pay their taxes, their fuel bills and their repair bills. It may well be that, to a party which coined the watchword "What's a million?", $200 may not be very much. But, Mr. Chairman, I assure you that by the people of my constituency it was gratefully received. I am sure that they would want me to say through you, Mr. Chairman, to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Agriculture that they appreciate the principle on which these payments were made, that they know they were based on an interim basis only and that more is to come. They know there is a long range program which is yet to come before the house. They have received the payments on that basis, and I think the payments have served a very useful purpose.

I do not think any member of this house can have any quarrel with the general purpose of this legislation which is to provide temporary assistance of a special kind to a special group of Canadians who are in need. After all, that is just a practical demonstration of the principle of bearing one another's burdens. But though we may be in agreement with the purpose and the principle embodied in this item, in my opinion there is room for some concern about the way in which these funds are to be disbursed.

Supply-Agriculture
Although the purpose of this item is to meet a need, nevertheless it is not going to be administered on the basis of need. As I understand it, this item will enable a payment of $200 to be made to every farmer, whether he needs it or not. In that connection there are two points which I should like to make and the first one is this. I suggest that $200 cannot be of much assistance to a farmer whose need is very great.
Oh, oh.
May I say that personally-
Personally you come from Newfoundland.
I come from Newfoundland where we have fishermen who need $200 a great deal more than do some of those who are going to get this payment but who do not need it at all.
I would recommend to the hon. member that he take a trip out west and find out.
The hon. member may rise and make his own speech when he is ready. I am making mine now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I am not a farmer but I know a great deal about fishermen and I know a good deal about their problems. As I said before, one payment of $200 cannot be of great significance to a farmer who does not need it at all but who is going to get it. Even if the farmer is in great need, $200 may not meet his requirements. As a good many members in this house have pointed out, $200 does not come anywhere near meeting the needs of some farmers whom these funds apparently are supposed to benefit. If we are going to dispense public funds, surely it would be better to pay them to those who really need them, and not to those who do not need them at all. If my hon. friend is in favour of paying out public funds to people who do not need assistance, that is for him to say. For my part, I am against it.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

I will answer questions when I am finished. The other point in connection with this legislation is this. I think we have reached a point in our economy where we must take a second look at our give-away programs and come to some decision on the question whether it is in the public interest to give public funds to anyone who does not need them.
Is that Liberal policy?

I think we should also consider whether or not our economy can continue to support that kind of administration of public funds. In two elections we were led to expect that a national policy would be developed, one which would apply equally to all Canadians and to all groups of Canadians. What I should like to see would be a policy developed. This is true particularly in respect of those of us who represent other primary producers, and I am thinking particularly of the fishermen whom I represent.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is now getting into the realm of economic policy and is departing from the resolution being discussed. Will the hon. member please try to confine his remarks to the resolution under discussion.

Mr. Chairman, I am trying to keep entirely within the rules of the house. What I am trying to base my argument on is the method by which this money is going to be disbursed as it is plainly written down here in the supplementary estimates, namely that it is going to go to everyone, whether he needs it or not. Those of us who represent other primary producers would be failing in our duty if, at a time when the government is prepared to give money to some people who do not need it, we did not rise and object that they have refused to pay it to those of our constituents who are really in great need.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on this item, may I say this. I have observed those hon. members who have spoken previously, particularly those in the official opposition. I have noted what they have said. May I say that I have felt sorry, to some degree, for the party that is trying to take issue without having a member on their side from western Canada.
We are doing all right.
Let the hon. member worry about himself.

I would make one recommendation to that party. If they ever intend or hope to get a member from western Canada I would suggest that they do not send the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate out to western Canada to campaign for them because if they did so I am certain that after the next election they would come back and still be in the same condition as that in which they are to-day.
To get back to the item under discussion, I should like to refer to the speech made by the Minister of Agriculture on January 23 and his statement that more people are dependent on the agriculture industry either

directly or indirectly than on any other industry in Canada. I think that statement should be kept in mind when this committee is talking about an increase in acreage payments. The hon. member for Assiniboia spoke on this subject and said he was greatly disappointed at the benefit this was bringing to western agriculture. He also said that when the government brought this in they assumed it would be a cure-all. Mr. Chairman, when this measure was brought in it was not intended to be a cure-all. I notice that the hon. member referred to this in his speech as a small payment; it was no longer "peanuts". It certainly was not, because this acreage payment means, to my constituency alone, approximately $1 million and I do not belong among those followers of Mr. C. D. Howe who agreed with him when he said "what's a million?" To me, a million is a whole lot of money, and to the farmers in my constituency a million is a whole lot of money.
In my constituency $200 is.

When this government took office in the fall of 1957, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said he hoped to export-and thought he could export-300 million bushels of wheat. I do not know what happened in Newfoundland, but in western Canada Liberals laughed and said: wait until he tries to sell some, he will find it a lot more difficult than he thinks.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Shall we get back to item 698?
I was dealing entirely with the wheat situation. To go along a little further, we did export 316 million bushels-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but we are not discussing the export of Canadian wheat. The matter under debate concerns this payment to western grain producers of $1 per acre to a maximum of $200, and the hon. member must limit his remarks to the item.

I am sorry if I have strayed from the item. I thought that in dealing with the wheat question I would get around to the fact that in exporting more wheat we improve substantially the position of farmers in western Canada. However, to get back to this acreage payment, let me say that there has been much discussion of the pros and cons. I have advocated a two-price system for wheat, and under this acreage plan up to a dollar a bushel more is allowed for wheat consumed in Canada-and I say that that is not "peanuts" either.
Perhaps I may quote what Mr. Wesson, president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, has to say about acreage payments:
Supply-Agriculture
Deficiency payments are not designed to aid failure or uneconomic farm units. Deficiency payments do not deal with relief; they are dealing with a marketing problem.
The report continues:
The acreage payment of $1 an acre by the government was a relief measure-a measure of temporary help, Mr. Wesson stated. It proved to him that many people had not yet recognized the real nature of the farm problem.
In a sense, Mr. Wesson never realized the real nature of the acreage payments, because it must be understood that the farmer benefited to the tune of a dollar a bushel more for wheat consumed in Canada. That is not a relief measure at all: it is direct aid to the farmers who, I might add, have produced wheat during the forties and sold it at about a dollar a bushel below the international wheat price, under the previous government.
Dealing with Mr. Wesson's statement that deficiency payments are not designed to aid failures or uneconomic units, I think this is the point at which an acreage payment does definitely bring some aid, namely to the uneconomic units, which are, after all, the units that we should try to help and pull up so that they can become economic units. There is no sense in taking honest dollars from the treasury to help a unit that is already a sound business. I want to help the small farmers who are caught in the cost-price squeeze as a result of which they are unable to make their places into economic units. Mr. Alf Gleave has scoffed and laughed at the acreage payment. I do not know whether he calls it "peanuts" or not. And yet in statements in the Saskatchewan papers in the Star-Phoenix he comes out with a plan. And what is it based on? An acreage system.
Mr. Charlie Gibbing, vice president of the Saskatchewan pool, is advocating a two-price system, which is, in essence what this acreage payment is.
We have heard a great deal from the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo who said that farmers did not want it and do not need it. I could go on all night as to how badly they have needed it and how much they want it. But to add a little more about the two-price system, I hope this government will either bring in an additional measure with regard to acreage payments next year or introduce a two-price system. This is sound business, and I notice recently that the President of the United States has proposed a similar two-price system for that country. I think this suggestion should be given a great deal of consideration. It might be that the price of bread will increase, and in this connection I notice that recently in Alberta the price of bread went up by a cent

Supply-Agriculture
a loaf and I never picked up one Alberta paper which objected too strongly in its editorial columns. I think that if we do not wish to continue paying out of the federal treasury we should charge it to the people who buy the bread, because I think the farmer in western Canada is in need of one dollar a bushel more for wheat consumed in Canada; I think it is coming to him.
On a point of privilege, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member who has just taken his seat put words into my mouth that I did not use. I did not say that farmers did not need it.
You certainly did.
No, no, I did not.
Yes, you did.
Oh no, I said this money was being paid to farmers whether they needed it or not, which is quite a different thing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member raised this as a question of privilege-

I am not objecting to payments being made to farmers who need them, but I was objecting to paying this money out to people who do not need it, and people who do not need it can get it under the way this system is administered at present.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am amused to know that we have now obtained more or less what we wanted-a two price system-and that the dollar a bushel would apply on our domestic consumption of wheat. However, I think the hon. member was referring to bread wheat consumed in Canada rather than to Canadian consumption as a whole. I wish to state very emphatically that we are in favour of the payment of this subsidy to western farmers. I believe it is very similar to the 5 cents a bushel Bennett paid during the depression in terms of present day purchasing power. In my opinion any amount paid to the farmers is of benefit to them.
I was out in western Canada this fall and everywhere I went I heard farmers say that the situation in their area was very grim. When one considers the price of tractors, food and other things one realizes that $200 is peanuts to the farmers. I am surprised that 200 acres should have been selected as a maximum. I am told that the average acreage of farms in Manitoba is 300 acres.
It is 235 in Manitoba.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I understand it is approximately 300 in Manitoba and approximately 500 in Saskatchewan.
I suggest that the hon. member read Hansard for September 6, 1958.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I would suggest that the hon. member make his own speech. In my opinion this payment is not a complete answer to the problem but we are in complete agreement that it should be paid. Any assistance given to the farmers is advantageous even if one must describe it as peanuts.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to bring you a note of good cheer from that great constituency of Moose Mountain which I have the honour to represent. I am pleased to state that the farmers in my area after examining the government's agricultural legislation over the past couple of years are very happy about it. In fact, in looking over the record I feel confident in saying that we have achieved more as a government in the last two years than the former government did in 22 years.
The farmers in my area are more than pleased with the acreage bonus now under discussion. I was interested in listening to the gloom and doom cast by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. In his opening remarks he states that he was not too conversant with farm problems and I agree with him.
I may say to the hon. member for Assini-boia who represents my neighbouring constituency that if he had stayed home a little more last fall in the interval between sessions instead of travelling across the country and making numerous appearances on television he would be more conversant with the opinion of farmers in his constituency. In fact I had the pleasure of discussing the acreage bonus legislation in his constituency with a great number of farmers in that area when I addressed a public meeting at Milestone. I did not hear a dissenting vote. Indeed I heard many favourable comments about this legislation.
One Tory meeting.

There is a growing awareness on the part of farmers about the beneficial results of this legislation. The hon. member for Assiniboia has been busy spreading gloom, doom and pessimism. He says that everything the government does is too little and too late. The people in that area, however, are becoming increasingly aware that the hon. member for Assiniboia preaches the doctrine of plausible nonsense. Those who are informed about the government's legislative program in relation to agriculture

are aware that what the hon. member says is utter nonsense and to those who are not informed it is plausible.
In considering the sum of $40 million it is important to focus our attention on the value of this money to the economy in the past year. Three years ago the farmers of western Canada through their organized farm groups, unions and so on suggested that they would be satisfied with parity prices. None of us was able to hit on a formula as to what an adequate parity price was and so we then talked about a two-price system. Last year, of course, representations were made to the federal government concerning the desirability of instituting deficiency payments. In effect the sum of $40 million represents the establishment of a two-price system if it is viewed in its true sense. This does not represent a complete answer to the problems of agriculture but it does represent the fulfilment of the promise of this government to agriculture that it would examine the problems and bring in temporary or emergency measures designed to put the farmers in a better position in relation to other Canadians.
We in Canada consume approximately 38 million bushels of wheat each year. Our price for No. 2 wheat last year in the west was between $1.15 and $1.22. Taking into consideration that we received $40 million in the form of acreage payments the government was actually paying the farmers of Canada approximately $2.25 a bushel for the wheat used for human consumption this year and that is not to be sneezed at. Having examined the operation of the legislation the farmers of western Canada are quite happy with it.
If I were to demand the latitude demanded by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate I could go on at great length discussing many other pieces of agricultural legislation to put the question of acreage bonus payments in its true perspective but I do not want to transgress the rules of the house. I believe the matter was extremely well covered by the Minister of Agriculture when he pointed out that last year our agricultural economy improved to the extent of 10 per cent whereas the cost of goods and services increased by only 1 per cent.
I thank the committee for its indulgence and I shall conclude by pointing out to hon. gentlemen that the present government is taking a positive and constructive approach towards the problems of agriculture. I am convinced that farmers by and large are quite happy with the legislative program of this government in relation to agriculture and are
Sup p ly-A griculture
equally happy about prospective agricultural legislation to be placed on the statute books in the future.

Mr. Chairman, for the last hour I have felt somewhat like a jack-in-the-box in my efforts to be recognized. I should like to add my voice to the others that have spoken out in general approval of the motion before us. I am certainly going to stick to the subject matter of this resolution in my brief remarks.
I have received letters, as I am sure all hon. members representing rural constituencies have, expressing approval of these payments. I have yet to hear of any farmer in Canada who sent these payments back to the government because he did not approve of them.
There has been much talk in this house about deficiency payments. Indeed there was much talk about them in Springfield. Some have said it would be much better to have deficiency payments than a payment of $1 an acre. In Springfield we went to the trouble of finding out exactly what deficiency payments would do for the farmers in the area. We took figures for our crop area which is crop district No. 5 in Manitoba. We found out that in 1957, the last year for which we had complete statistics, there were 2,232,000 bushels of wheat harvested. During the years 1940 to 1954 this area marketed 52.8 per cent of the grain produced. In other words the other 47.2 per cent was kept for seed, was fed to livestock, or disposed of by other means and was not sold at the elevator.
Under the principle of deficiency payments the money would be paid only on wheat marketed at the elevator. On the basis of marketings of 52.8 per cent in this crop district the farmers sold 1,178,000 bushels of wheat at the elevator or 290 bushels for each of the 4,065 farmers shown by the 1956 census to be residing in this area.
The marketing of barley and oats arrived at by a similar calculation totalled 120 bushels and 148 bushels per farmer. On the basis of 1957 production, and the marketing percentages that have been typical for the area over the period of 15 years this would provide a gross average of $133 per farm based on the proposed deficiency payment in the year for which the highest level was suggested which was 1956-57. This was 30 cents a bushel for wheat, 19 cents a bushel for barley and 15 cents a bushel for oats. So on the basis of deficiency payments the farmers of Springfield would have received an average of $133.
What about the farmer who was hailed out, the farmer who had a crop failure or

Supply-Agriculture
the farmer who, like the many mentioned by the Minister of Agriculture, fed his grain to livestock and did not market any? The fact is that those farmers who were most in need of help would not have received anything. I know at least one farmer in Saskatchewan who farms 26 sections of land. On this basis, had we adopted deficiency payments it would have brought thousands and thousands of dollars into the hands of those large farmers. There is nothing wrong with that, but on the basis of the money which was made available-$40 million-I submit it was most equitable to distribute the money in the manner in which it was distributed.
Some members of the official opposition suggested that they were opposed to this and this applies especially to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I am most surprised at this, since he is a former Manitoban. We certainly would be depriving many farmers in Manitoba of money which they need very badly if we should cut out the additional amount which the minister has brought forward today.

I never said any such
thing.

Another hon. member suggested it was a handout pure and simple. For years the farmers of western Canada have been subsidizing the bread-eaters of Canada. If we show the western farmers that we wish to give them a little benefit at a time when they are in dire need I certainly think it will be appreciated.

Mr. Chairman, I am rising on a question of privilege to correct a statement made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I am sure he made it mistakenly and inadvertently but he suggested that I was opposing this item. I have never said a word in opposition to it. I said that this policy should be applied all across Canada to all groups, and that is my position.

My remarks on this item
will be very brief. On other occasions I may speak a little longer. I want to make it clear at the outset that I am not opposing this measure to provide for payments of $1 per acre up to a maximum of $200 per farm to western grain producers; but before this item passes I would like the Minister of Agriculture to tell us why other groups of primary producers should be excluded from similar measures. If the principle is established for the western grain producers, and if it is considered to be a good principle for the country, why would it not be good for our eastern farmers and our eastern fishermen? Why should it not apply to a farmer who

cuts pulpwood on his wood lot and has to accept a price of $8 or $9 a cord at the roadside, as happened in New Brunswick in 1958? I know that the farmers of my constituency would be satisfied to accept 25 per cent of the amount which was-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On a point of order, surely, Mr. Chairman, we can, after all the admonitions that have been heard from the Chair this afternoon and this evening on the subject of adhering to the point under discussion, ask the hon. member to stop wandering around and come to the point of the item, namely an addition to the amount already voted for the purpose of providing acreage payments for western wheat producers. This does not give licence to any member to start comparing this with other measures in other fields entirely. This is a matter, the principle of which has already been approved, Mr. Chairman, and $40 million has been disbursed. It is a matter now of deciding whether those who qualify and for whom there is not quite enough money are going to be treated as have those who have already received their acreage payments. This gives licence to no member to talk about everything under the sun except the acreage payments to western wheat producers.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He is following the example he had from over there.

I suggest there should be one ruling in this house for both sides of the house. We have just heard from the hon. member for Springfield and from two or three other hon. gentlemen up in this corner speeches of some length about deficiency payments and other alternative methods of doing this thing and not one word of protest was heard from the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Agriculture. The moment that anyone on this side of the house merely suggests that the national policy that the government boasts about should be a national policy a point of order is raised at once. Surely, in this free parliament fishermen can be mentioned.

I was just saying, when the Minister of Finance interrupted-and he is quite fast in blaming other members although he does interrupt so often himself-that the farmers in my

constituency would have been pleased to accept 25 per cent of the $800,000 which was paid under this measure to the constituents of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin.

Mr. Chairman, we are debating the addition of $1.3 million to an already approved item of $40 million to assist the farmers of western Canada, and it is on this subject that I wish to speak briefly this evening.
Why was the money paid; why was the $40 million authorized by this house? It was authorized because the farmers of western Canada, or many of them, are in dire financial straits. In other words, the purchasing power of the farmers of western Canada is seriously injured. Let me say this. As a group, the farmers of western Canada, and any farming group, operate in an almost perfect economy; in other words, in perfect competition. No other group operates under a system under which they are unable to obtain for themselves the benefits of technological improvements. In other words the farmer of western Canada does not really realize that he is in competition with his neighbour in the production of grain. Therefore, we must subsidize the farmer in order that he may have the purchasing power needed to buy the things that he needs today and which he finds difficulty in buying because of the cost-price squeeze. On the one hand there is the cost of machinery and on the other low income from wheat. It is this cost-price squeeze that occasions the difficulties in which the farmers find themselves in this country today.
There has been a lot of talk here tonight about the cordwood people and fishermen and that they should be given a subsidy. Almost everybody who has anyone in his constituency who is unemployed or who has any small group in difficulty feels that those people should be given subsidies. We are talking tonight about a large group, a group of farmers in western Canada, who have need of purchasing power to-day, not to-morrow or next week. What has this government done about it? They have appropriated $40 million to assist the farmers of western Canada with their purchases. Let me say this. In a cross-section of farmers of western Canada you will find probably a small percentage whose operations have been profitable; you will find a middle-sized group and you will
Supply-Agriculture
find a still larger group of small farmers who need financial assistance, who need the help of this government. The sum of $40 million was appropriated. Judging by the thinking and utterances of my hon. friends opposite one would think that it was not appreciated by the farmers of western Canada.
I recall one instance, for example. One farmer in my constituency, and there are many more like him, was hailed out in six successive years. When he got his $200 cheque he looked at it, saw all the holes in it, put it on his player piano and it played for him, "Happy Days are Here Again". Most every western community has at least 500 farmers and if you multiply 500 by $200 you get $100,000 in purchasing power in each such community. It is that purchasing power which has helped the retailer, the physician, in fact, all groups of society, and has really kept our society going.
Finally, some have spoken of the $200 payment to the farmer as being peanuts. All I would say to them is: Come on out to my constituency and talk to the people. It is true that this is only a temporary measure to meet a certain situation and that with the passing of time it will be necessary to give careful examination to all phases of agriculture. It has already been indicated that two of them, farm credit and crop insurance, will be dealt with at this session.
I believe we are coming to a time when certain farmers in western Canada will need help. There are others who will not. A differential payment was necessary and I want to compliment the government for having paid out the money on an acreage basis thus making it possible for the small farmer to benefit rather than having a large portion of the money paid to the big operators. In other words, all the farmers received something and I can assure the house that the people of western Canada appreciate deeply what their government has done.

I should like to speak very briefly on this item. First, I should like to say that the principle of deficiency payments to those in need is one which must receive the approval of every civilized and humane person. Probably nothing is more disappointing and demoralizing than a crop failure. Those people who had hoped to reap and found that there was nothing in their fields to reap must appreciate deeply the special assistance from the government which avoids for them the shame of relief. I have just one comment to make. I regret deeply that the standard which applies to those who till the soil seems not to apply to those who plow the fields of the Atlantic.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in this free-wheeling debate it is hardly necessary for me to add anything to the very comprehensive statement on this subject made a short time ago by the Minister of Agriculture. However, I was very interested in what the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River said. He spoke on the gold subsidy and a variety of other subjects. I have always had a great admiration for the hon. gentleman's debating ability and I find that I am in agreement with the statement he made in opening his remarks that he did not know anything about agriculture. I did not hear all the remarks of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate but I believe that he too said that he knew little or nothing about the farm problem, and I am inclined to agree that as a farmer he is a poor fisherman. However, this can be expected from two gentlemen, who, as I have said, have admitted that they are not-
