I think that the hon. member for Assiniboia forgets that over two-thirds of the farmers in western Canada farm less than 300 acres.
I should like to refer to a speech made by the Minister of Agriculture on October 28, 1957, found at page 462 of Hansard, in which he gave a breakdown of the size of the farms. This is relevant to the acreage payments under discussion. He gave a breakdown of the permit holders and their acreages. He said that there were a total of 230,854 permit holders and that of this total 31,299 had less than 99 specified acres or acres under cultivation, 63,272 had between 100 and 199 acres and 51,762 had between 200 and 299 acres under cultivation.
Therefore, in trying to do something to help to relieve the farmers of the cost-price

squeeze the government had to take into consideration, and wisely so, the fact that the majority of the farmers were small farmers, and the acreage payments made by the government recognized the fact that every farmer and his family are of equal importance to our nation. The payments also take into consideration the fact that the costs of production on small farms are higher and provide that the man who is able to harvest no crop or only a small crop on account of the weather will also be paid. Therefore I think that the government followed a very wise course in setting up a system of acreage payments. Payments are made to small farmers on an equal basis and are particularly helpful to the farmer whose costs of production are high.
I do not know how the hon. member for Assiniboia is going to justify the fact that he is in favour of deficiency payments. I should like him to justify deficiency payments on grain in comparison with the principle of acreage payments because, as I say, I think the acreage payment has been justified and will help the largest number of farmers who really need it.

Mr. Chairman, between this session and the last session of this house I happened to do what so many of the government members have advised the hon. member for Assiniboia to do, I stayed home and tended to my knitting. As a result of the fact there is not very much wheat grown in the riding of Timmins I must confess I do not know too much about the situation in the west. However, I have listened very carefully to the debate so far, and the speeches made by the minister and the government members from the west who represent all but one riding from western Canada. I am referring, of course, to the three wheat provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that there are two things that have been established very clearly by government spokesmen today, not only established but reiterated time and again. The first is that the farmers in the west are better off now than they have ever been since the war. Secondly, this $200 bonus that they got last year was the greatest thing that happened to them since the war. Before this debate is concluded, I should like to have some government member explain this to me. I find it difficult to understand how, if they are having the best times they have ever had, this $200 is so important.

I think the views of government members have been very clearly explained here tonight, and I should like to voice my approval of this supplementary

acreage payment. I should like also to thank the Minister of Agriculture for his clear explanation of the need for this extra $1,300,000 to pay some of the farmers who did not have their permit books when the payment was first announced. I think this will clear up a situation that some of our western members have had to face, and about which the farmers have been writing to them.
In so far as this debate is concerned, we have had some amazing statements. I do not believe I am out of order in referring to the mass delegation that is coming down here. I should like to say that I am quite sure the government will receive them and give them a courteous hearing. I should like to refer to statements made about these acreage payments by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, and to put them on the record. He said it was a great sum of money; he was against special handouts to any special group; the needs of the Newfoundland fishermen are much greater than those of the western farmers. I am not quite sure whether the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is speaking personally or for his party. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said that this supplementary payment applies only to a limited group; that the people in Canada are becoming alarmed at the increasing demands on government for handouts. The member for Burin-Burgeo said that he came from Newfoundland where there are fishermen who need the $200 a great deal more than the farmers do. He asked, how long can our economy support this kind of giveaway?
I just wanted to put these statements on the record, Mr. Chairman, because they will make good reading for the farmers who are coming down here in this mass delegation.

I feel I should say a few words on this item because a considerable amount of the money that is going to be required initially is going to be required in my constituency where we have the greatest number of small farmers in western Canada. They are all very small farmers, who are on the edge of the cultivated area. I am sure the people in my area would like me to tell the minister how much they appreciate the principle enunciated in making these acreage payments.
For the information of the hon. member for Assiniboia, I should like to say that the wheat board has now corrected its stand and all the people who are growing grain for feeding to cattle can receive acreage payments as soon as their acreage has been checked. I was interested, too, in the Liberal approach to this problem. I think that the most we can gather from it is that they are back to their old tactics of dividing this country in the
Supply-Agriculture
hope that they can conquer it. I feel that their speeches will tend towards disunity, and the speeches made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the hon. member for Burin - Burgeo were excellent examples. We in the west realize that Newfoundland has its problems, and we are willing to listen to those problems. We feel that when we are talking about a western problem, acreage payments, they should at least have the courtesy to discuss that item.

I listened with a great deal of interest to the comments that have been made by hon. members this evening. As has already been pointed out by the hon. member for Timmins, it is a rather sad reflection on the economic position of western agriculture if the $200 payment is so important in relation to their income. I am not one of those who feels that this is the best method of assisting western agriculture. It is true that this payment goes to a great many small farmers.
On the one hand, the government says we are going to help the small farmers. This is the way to help the small farmers. If you proceed by way of deficiency payments, you will not help the small farmers. Then, they say we will put a $200 ceiling on these payments. The only people who do not get the $200 payment are the small farmers. Anyone who has a medium sized farm or a big farm gets the maximum payment, but the small farmer gets less than $200. However, these are the people who say this is the measure to help the small farmer.
For what are the people of western Canada asking? Are they asking for this? Is this the thing upon which the government campaigned? I never heard this particular measure mentioned anytime in the election campaign. I never heard any reference made by any Conservative speaker to a dollar an acre payment. However, the Prime Minister was giving sympathetic consideration to deficiency payments. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and I had this out the other day, but a report of a speech he made at Wolseley stated that action was going to be taken on deficiency payments. When we asked the government during the session last year whether they were considering deficiency payments, they said they were considering deficiency payments; sincere consideration; thorough consideration; adequate consideration; daily consideration. Did one member from that party last year stand up and say to the Prime Minister, we do not want deficiency payments; we do not think that is what should be done. No, they waited like mice until the Prime Minister made the announcement.

Supply-Agriculture
I object to that statement.

My friend is a very loud mouse, but I am always pleased to hear him. They waited as quiet as mice, shall we say, and they did not mention deficiency payments. They waited until the line was laid down. Then when the $200 acreage payment was announced they tallied about the wonderful Prime Minister and the great action he was taking for agriculture. This was the line.
Well, the line is being changed. Now we hear it being said in places that perhaps we should have a two-price system. I wonder if word has gone out via the grapevine that this thing is in the cards, that this is the thing the government is going to do. If the farmers of western Canada are so much in favour of this answer to their problem, I wonder how it happens that they are organizing a mass delegation which, I am informed, is very close to being 100 per cent signed up. More important than that is the fact that people are contributing their money in order to finance the cost of that delegation coming to Ottawa.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Assiniboia has the floor.

The farm organizations of
western Canada have now said what they wish the government to do. There is not a farm organization that has gone on record as being in favour of the dollar an acre payment as an answer to western agriculture. As a matter of fact, when the Prime Minister announced this payment last year initially, I at that time quoted Mr. James Patterson, president of the Manitoba farmers' union and president of the interprovincial farm union council at the point at which he said just how inadequate this measure was. In order to have on the record the first clear indication of what organized agriculture thought of this payment I should like to refer again to that statement found at page 4350 of Hansard of August 30, 1958, as follows:
We certainly expected something reasonable . . . and the $25 million-
I might say that was the initial press report; it was since corrected to $40 million.
-falls far short ... It takes a long time to pay bills with nickels.
This responsible leader of the farm movement did not call it peanuts, he called it nickels. He went on to say this:
It will give the farmer a little "spending money" said Mr. Patterson, and the government apparently thinks that will settle matters for a while.

In asking for an alternative to this proposal, the farm organizations are asking on the last crop a deficiency payment of 36 cents a bushel from which a farmer who markets 600 bushels of wheat would obtain more than $200. A farmer who ordinarily produces 600 bushels of wheat cannot get $200 under the present legislation.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.
What would the farmer who did not raise any wheat or who did not sell any wheat get under your deficiency payment plan?
The deficiency payment plan is based on the price of wheat. It is a good question, a fair question and one that should be dealt with.
The hon. member has not yet answered the question.

If my hon. friend will relax for a minute, I shall be happy to answer it. The question is what will a person get who does not sell a bushel of wheat under the deficiency payment plan. The answer to that question is that under the deficiency payment plan advocated by farm organizations in western Canada today, farmers would be paid on the basis of the price of wheat. It is not an acreage payment. In order to obtain the benefit, it would be necessary for a farmer to sell wheat.
He would have to grow wheat.
Of course. If you want to get payment for a bushel of wheat you must have a bushel of wheat. It is just as simple as that.
And a man who is hailed out would get nothing.

We know that farmers need payment when they have a crop failure. Certainly they need income when they have nothing to sell. That should be done through extension of the prairie farm assistance payments. It should be handled in the way of compensation to the farmers who have had a crop failure.
The whole point that western agriculture is making at this time is with respect to the efficient farmer, to say nothing of the inefficient farmer because he has a small unit through no fault of his own. The highly mechanized efficient farmer, with present costs and present prices, is unable to make an adequate living. They are saying that in order to give the grain producer a chance to make a standard of living in keeping with

Business of the House
Canadian conditions he should be paid a deficiency payment to compensate for the tremendous increase in the cost of production that has taken place in recent years. Hon. members may laugh if they wish at those organizations which are promoting this suggestion, but I would remind them that the whole program of deficiency payments today is supported by the three western wheat pools, by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, by the farmers' union and by every bona fide national farm organization in this country. In order to show their complete support for this proposition they are circulating in western Canada a petition that is getting an almost 100 per cent sign-up.
That is not true.

Not only is this program getting support amongst the farmers but step by step, as it is taken to other farm organizations, it is receiving support. From the largest farm organization in Canada, namely the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, which met the other day in Saskatoon, there came a motion which was passed supporting the farmers' program, with one delegate voting against it.
